item.title: Agent sessions now run in shelley.service at oom_score_adj -1: test_sessions_here_are_killable red on the host
item.body:
Found while shipping #392 (2026-10-24). The ship gate went red on a test #392 didn't touch, and the failure reproduces on `origin/main` `0a612ce`. #392 shipped with this one test deselected, by operator decision.

## Observation `[measured, 2026-10-24 ~03:40Z]`

`tests/deploy/test_earlyoom_decline.py::test_sessions_here_are_killable` fails on the host:

> no exe.dev session root above this process — neither a child of ['exe-init', 'sshd'] nor a PID 1 child in /init.scope … if it was run from one, exe.dev changed how a session starts and this walk needs to learn it (#333)

The agent session's process chain, from this Shelley conversation:

```
bash     oom_score_adj=-1  /system.slice/shelley.service
bash     oom_score_adj=-1  /system.slice/shelley.service
shelley  oom_score_adj=-1  /system.slice/shelley.service   (PPid 1)
```

`systemctl show shelley`: `FragmentPath=/etc/systemd/system/shelley.service`, `OOMScoreAdjust=-1`, `ActiveEnterTimestamp=Fri 2026-10-23 04:45:38 UTC`.

So Shelley sessions now run inside a **system service**. They aren't under `exe-init`/`sshd` or in `/init.scope`, and they start at `oom_score_adj` **-1**, not the `SESSION_ADJ = 0` the earlyoom decline rests on (docs/HOST-MEMORY.md §3, #337).

## Questions

1. **Is this an exe.dev platform change** (Shelley moved into a unit) or a local one? The unit appeared or restarted 2026-10-23 04:45Z; check `exe-init --version` and the unit's provenance. Only documented exe.dev behaviour counts.
2. **Does the earlyoom decline still hold?** -1 is barely below 0, so the kernel can still pick a session. But it now shares a cgroup with the Shelley server, and `MemoryLow`/slice placement (#307, #309) may differ from what HOST-MEMORY.md assumes. Re-read the reservation math against `system.slice/shelley.service`.
3. **Teach the walk:** should `shelley.service` count as a session root, with its expected adj? Or should the test fail-with-guidance as it does now, the #333 rule being to gate on the host and never on the thing under test? Either way, the gate must be runnable from the agent session that ships, or the procedure has to name the SSH session it needs.

## Done when

- [ ] Questions 1–2 answered, with readings recorded here.
- [ ] `test_sessions_here_are_killable` passes from a Shelley session on the host, or the ship procedure documents where it must run, with no deselect needed.
- [ ] docs/HOST-MEMORY.md updated if the premise moved.

item.title: DB CHECK: entity_subtype consistent with entity_type (after #206 backfill)
item.body:
From the #206 code review (round 3, item 13). Follows #206; do after its Task 1.6 backfill.

**Problem.** Migration 0009 constrains `entities.entity_subtype` to the seven values (or NULL), but nothing ties it to `entity_type`. The database would accept `person` + `business`, or `organization` + NULL. Today only `entity_classification.resolve_entities()` writes these columns, and it keeps them consistent. A hand edit, or a later code path that bypasses the resolver, could store an inconsistent pair. #209's subtype filter and badge assume the pairing.

**Why not in 0009.** Until the Task 1.6 backfill runs, every existing organization (1,391 on prod) has a NULL subtype. A cross-column CHECK added in 0009 would fail on prod data.

**Proposal.** A new migration, after 1.6 is applied on prod:

```sql
ALTER TABLE entities ADD CONSTRAINT ck_entities_subtype_matches_type CHECK (
  (entity_type = 'organization' AND entity_subtype IS NOT NULL)
  OR (entity_type <> 'organization' AND entity_subtype IS NULL)
);
```

`entity_type <> 'organization'` covers `person` and the legacy `''`. Precheck on prod:

```sql
SELECT entity_type, entity_subtype IS NULL, count(*) FROM entities GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

It should return no organization row with a NULL subtype and no person row with a subtype. Consider the same rule on `entity_classifications` (`organization` ⇒ subtype; `person` / `not_a_name` ⇒ NULL). `record_manual` already validates it for manual rows.

**Done when:** migration plus a `test_schema.py` case for each rejected pair; SCHEMA.md updated.

item.title: FYI: address-validator Tailscale restart, 2026-10-23 between 14:15 and 15:00 UTC (~2 s outbound DNS blip; API stays up)
item.body:
address-validator takes Tailscale 1.102.4 → 1.104.2 for TS-2026-013 (the eMudhra compromise; CannObserv/address-validator#345). The window is **2026-10-23 between 14:15 and 15:00 UTC**, and the restart itself lasts about 2 s (measured at 2.0–2.3 s on four sibling hosts).

- **The API stays up.** Callers reach it through the exe.dev proxy, not the tailnet, and the service isn't restarted.
- **What can blip:** MagicDNS owns this host's resolver, so outbound DNS for its USPS and Google provider calls fails for those ~2 s. A request that misses cache in that moment can come back `unavailable` (fail-open). Parse/standardize and cached results are unaffected.
- **What you do:** nothing. Any row stamped `unavailable` inside the window is picked up by your normal re-check. Exact timestamps follow on CannObserv/address-validator#345.

item.title: Verify: first scheduled entity-classification run (2026-10-25) and first prod not-a-name purge (from #205)
item.body:
Two checks left over from #205 (Jev entity classification). Neither could run before the epic closed.

## 1. Due 2026-10-25 ≈ 11:00Z: the first *scheduled* weekly classification run

`wslcb-entity-classification.timer` fires Sun 04:00 America/Los_Angeles plus up to 5 min jitter (`systemctl list-timers` showed 11:02:38Z on 2026-10-23T23:25Z). Until now only manual starts have run it.

Check after ≈ 11:10Z:
```bash
systemctl show wslcb-task@classify-entities.service -p Result -p ExecMainStartTimestamp
journalctl -u wslcb-task@classify-entities --since '2026-10-25 10:55' -o cat --no-pager | tail -20
```
- **Expect:** `Result=success`, a check-in `202 Accepted`, and `ok` with `enabled=true`.
- **Expect `names_sent`** to equal the entities created since the 2026-10-23 backfill. The relayed import's post-ingest pass normally classifies those first, so expect ≈ 0, with backlog 0.
- **Afterwards,** co-status's `co-wslcb-classify` deadline moves to ≈ 2026-11-01T14:0xZ (7 d 3 h after this check-in). It is currently 2026-10-30T23:16:39Z.
- **If the run alerts:** `metadata.fault` names the cause. See `docs/MONITORING.md` § Entity classification check-in.

## 2. On trigger: the first purge of a confirmed non-name on prod

#206 never exercised purge and link renumbering on prod data: prod had no noise entities. It runs the first time an operator uses **Not a name** on `/admin/entities/review` and then someone runs `wslcb db reclassify-entities`.

When that happens:
- run the `--dry-run` first, and check that `confirmed_noise` matches the entities marked;
- after the apply, check the entity is gone, its record links are renumbered, and `uv run wslcb db check` is unchanged;
- run it outside the ingest windows (≈ 07:33–07:45Z and 13:30–13:45Z, +1 h after 2026-11-01).

Close this issue once both checks have passed.

item.title: coordinating-epics: the note op joins with a bare space, so a note runs into the line's last field
item.body:
Child of #404. Found at that epic's first check-in, the first real `epic-edit.sh` write in this repo.

**What:** the `note` op appends its text to the line after a single space (`_epic_edit.py`, the `note` branch of `apply_ops`). Checklist lines separate their fields with ` · `, so a note runs into the line's last field:

```text
- [ ] #398 … say whether the Python engines are the unit Brief posted 2026-10-15 (…).
```

check-in.md §7's own example, `{"op": "note", "ref": "#45", "text": "Shipped 1a2b3c4..5d6e7f8, live {today}."}`, produces exactly this. #404's first write got around it by leading each note's text with `· ` by hand [measured: the dry-run diff, then the written body].

**Why it matters:** every check-in writes notes, and a coordinator who follows the documented example gets a line where the note reads as part of the title or the last field. The workaround has to be remembered on every op.

**Suggested fix:**
- Join with ` · ` when the line doesn't already end in a separator. A table row's last cell keeps its own rule (the CR 286 branch), and is worth a decision of its own: a cell may want ` · ` too, or a plain space.
- Keep the "already on the line" check (CR 253) working: it compares by the line's end, so it must compare against the joined form.
- Accept a text that already starts with `·` without doubling it, so epics written with the workaround stay idempotent.
- Update the template's "Notes on a line" bullet and check-in.md §7's example to show the result.

Tests: a note on a checklist item, a bullet and a table row; a repeated note (no-op); and a note whose text starts with `·`.

item.title: coordinating-epics: scan.sh lists the epic itself under new_numbers on the first check-in after creation
item.body:
Child of #404. Found at that epic's first check-in, the first real `scan.sh` run in this repo.

**What:** `scan.sh` lists the epic itself under `new_numbers` on the first check-in after the epic is created. The number walk in `_scan.py` keeps every number above the watermark, the epic included. The updated-since walk skips the epic (`if it["number"] == a.epic: continue`) and reports the epic's comments separately, as `epic_comments`.

Seen on #404: its header was written at creation with `Last issue seen: #403`, the highest number when the body was drafted. The first scan reported #404 as a new issue with `in_epic: false` and `mentions_epic: false`, the same shape as an unslotted follow-up [measured].

**Why it matters:** `epic-edit.sh --scan` already discounts the epic (its `new_issues` filter drops `a.epic`), so nothing is refused. But the report is what the coordinator reads to slot new work. A row that looks unslotted has to be recognised and explained every time. #404's log line had to say "the number walk lists #404 itself, which the editor discounts".

It happens whenever the epic's number is above the watermark: every epic created from a drafted body, since the body can't name its own number as already seen.

**Suggested fix:**
- In the number walk, skip `a.epic` the way updated-since does.
- Keep it in `max_number`, so `{last_seen}` still moves the watermark past the epic and the next walk doesn't stop on it.
- Test with the fake `gh` rig: a watermark below the epic's number gives no epic row, and `max_number` includes it.

item.title: coordinating-epics: scan.sh's updated-since cursor can lose an update GitHub's listing briefly leaves out
item.body:
Child of #404. Found at that epic's second check-in.

**What:** `scan.sh`'s updated-since cursor trusts one call to GitHub's issue listing (`repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues?state=all&since=…`), and that listing can leave out an issue updated minutes earlier. Then `{checked}` moves `Last check-in` past the missed update, and no later scan reports it.

**Seen on #404** [measured], with `since` 2026-10-15T15:30:06Z in both scans:

| Scan at | `updated_since` | |
|---|---|---|
| 15:45:48Z | #398, #399, #400, #405, #406 | #395 missing |
| 15:46:14Z | #395, #398, #399, #400, #405, #406 | |

#395 had been updated at 15:31:42Z, by a comment posted in the same loop as the comments on #398, #399 and #400, which the first scan did list. Three direct calls to the listing, between the two scans, all returned #395. Nothing in `_scan.py` filters the row out: the loop keeps every issue the listing returns except the epic. So the gap was GitHub's.

**Why it matters:** this cursor exists to catch what the number watermark can't: a reply on a closed child, a late approval, a gate flipped in another thread (check-in.md §3). A missed row isn't late, it's lost, because the next window starts at `{checked}`. Here the missed update was only the coordinator's own comment. On a live epic it could be an implementer's reply or the operator's go-ahead. #404 got through only because the coordinator re-scanned, and wrote with the second report.

Related: creation.md already warns that list queries lag right after bulk label edits (private-launch 35). This is the same lag without a bulk edit.

**Suggested fix (to weigh):**
- **Overlap the window.** Query `since` minus a margin (some minutes), while `{checked}` stays the scan's own time. Rows inside the margin come back again; that costs a re-read, not a miss.
- **Cross-check the epic's own items.** For each item in the epic, compare its `updated_at` (one call each, or one GraphQL query) against `since`, and add any the listing missed, flagged as such in `warnings`. This catches the rows that matter most even when the listing lags past the margin.
- Check whether the per-issue comment listings (`new_comments`, `epic_comments`) need the same overlap.
- Keep CR 265 and CR 276's guards right: a row the overlap brings back from above the old watermark still has to be mentioned.

Test with the fake `gh` rig: a listing that leaves out an epic item whose own `updated_at` is inside the window. The report must still carry that item.

item.title: coordinating-epics: replace-section on a ## heading also replaces its ### subsections
item.body:
Follow-up to gregoryfoster/skills#404 (coordinating-epics v1.1). Found while adopting CannObserv/watcher#368 with `epic-edit.sh` (fef0611), 2026-10-15.

**What:** `section_span` (`scripts/_epic_edit.py`) ends a section at the next heading of the **same or a shallower** level. So a `##` section's span includes every `###` subsection beneath it, and `replace-section` on the `##` heading replaces those subsections too.

**Seen on:** CannObserv/watcher#368. Its body had prose under `## Coordination`, followed by `### Child epics`, `### Cutover` and `### Issues`, with the whole checklist under `### Issues`. Replacing only the Coordination prose would have deleted the checklist. The dry run showed it. The workaround was to rewrite the entire tail as one `replace-section`, generated from the live body so the checklist lines were copied verbatim, and to promote the subsections to `##`. It worked (`readback: matches`, counts unchanged), but the operation's blast radius was the whole checklist.

**Why it matters:** an adopted epic is written outside the template, so it can nest its checklist under a prose heading. Anyone using `replace-section` to tidy the prose then deletes the children. The count check only catches it when the subsections hold checkboxes. Prose subsections disappear silently.

**Suggested fix (pick one):**
- `replace-section` refuses when the span contains a deeper heading, and names the subsections. Add a `--include-subsections` opt-in, or a `"scope": "own"|"tree"` field on the op.
- Or default to the section's **own** body, up to the next heading of any level, with `"scope": "tree"` to take the whole subtree.

Either way, `add-section` with `before` and `section_level` keep today's meaning. One test for each: a `##` with a `###` child, replaced with each scope.

item.title: patching-hosts process log: 2026-10-15 usa-wa, the sixth run under the scripts (#313 step 8b)
item.body:
Process-log entry for CannObserv/usa-wa's first run under the skill (CannObserv/usa-wa#497), drafted in the host repo per process-log.md § Adding an entry: the skill is vendored there, so this repo adds the file. Counts and families only; every package in it is applied.

**File:** `skills/patching-hosts/references/process-log/2026/2026-10-15-usa-wa.md`

**Index row** (`process-log/2026/index.md`):

```
| [2026-10-15](2026-10-15-usa-wa.md) | usa-wa | Sixth run, out of cycle (a knob copy added the day); the may-2026 image. 100 + Tailscale in the maintenance lane, 560 s (3.1× dry run); 19 s down. fwupd's conffile trap on may-2026 too, purged by hand; the alias remote leaves a tree's owner unknown |
```

---

## Session 2026-10-15 — usa-wa

The sixth run under the scripts, and this host's first (#313 step 8b; CannObserv/usa-wa#497). Its step 0 hand-run was CannObserv/usa-wa#430. It's the **`may-2026`** image, the generation between Feb-2026 and the newer ones, with a local PostgreSQL 16 whose own nightly backup to GCS stood in for the dump. The run was **out of cycle**: the owner took it on a Thursday, outside the knob's Tue/Wed window.

### Environment

- exe.dev, `exe-dev-exeuntu`, generation `may-2026`: `exe-setup.service` present, no `exeuntu` binary. The journal is persistent (42 days). `/tmp` is under Ubuntu's `D` rule, so the boot clears it.
- PostgreSQL 16 from Ubuntu main, C.UTF-8 on libc everywhere. The host's backup unit (`pg_dump -Fc`, verified, shipped create-only, sandboxed with no capabilities) covers the production database. Five pytest databases are excepted.
- A daily timer chain from 05:45 to ~11:30 UTC. The API serves published datasets to one public caller, which pulls at 09:00.
- Posture `scheduled`, window Tue + Wed 16:00–23:30 UTC (09:00–16:30 PDT / 08:00–15:30 PST, so DST moves nothing).

### Readings

- **The knob**, committed for this run, declares:
  - one `quiet` range per timer, from 5 min before `OnCalendar=` to its `RandomizedDelaySec=` plus the service's `TimeoutStartSec=`. The host repo's test derives each range from the unit files, so a moved timer fails its suite;
  - `inflight` as running `usa-wa-*` oneshots (`activating`), less the one `RemainAfterExit=yes` unit, plus a listener on the dev-server port;
  - the Postgres data store, and the backup line covering it;
  - Tailscale as `follow`, with its own `hold`;
  - one caller, and no `image-owner` (#350).
- **The first probe had 12 findings:**
  - Tailscale's origin had no policy, and its auto-update was on. Fixed: `follow`, a tracked pin file (site 100, client and keyring 600), and auto-update off on the node and for the tailnet;
  - `database:` ×5 for the pytest databases, and `datastore:` for an agent's code-search Qdrant: excepted;
  - `restarters:unread` ×4: excepted as `not-restarter`, each read first. One of them is `python -m <module>`, which the scan labels as a relative path (#393).
- **The maintenance lane's dry run exited 1 on fwupd's conffile prompt.** This image deleted `/etc/update-motd.d/85-fwupd` too, which the profile states for Feb-2026 only (#392). It was purged with the same 53 orphans as wslcb's, by hand, since `prune-plan.sh` has no apt mode (#370). The re-probe had **0 findings**.
- **The language class read owner `unknown`**: the probe reads a tree's owner from its git origin and misses the cohort's deploy-key alias remote (#391). An `owner <dir> self` line works around it. The tree had **42 advisories in 9 packages**, and the repo had no update mechanism; that's its own follow-up.
- **ESM:** 28 esm-apps updates visible; Pro isn't attached.
- **The pending set grew 45 → 48 security in the day between dry runs.** The run's dry run counted 101 (48 security, 52 `-updates`, Tailscale) in 181 s, max RSS 265 MB, a 137 MB download.
- **A reboot was certain before the apply:** PID 1 mapped 6 packages in the set.
- **The recovery point:** `recovery-point.sh` started the backup unit, which shipped a fresh dump in 3 s. The owner attested the object off the node.
- **The bulk took 100 in 560 s** (3.1× the dry run, just over the 3× the span budgets). Nothing was auto-removed. `/ready` answered 290 of 290 probes during it, and no service restarted. journald restarted mid-apply (systemd's upgrade).
  - Security families: systemd, OpenSSL, OpenSSH, sudo, libxml2, Kerberos, BIND, curl, libX11, libpng, FreeType, poppler, librsvg, libheif, libevent, python3-requests, python3-urllib3, python3-jwt, sg3-utils.
  - `-updates` families: AppArmor, apport, base-files, iproute2, Mesa, open-iscsi, open-vm-tools, plymouth, procps, snapd, tzdata, among others.
- **The `tailscale` step** took 15 s, at the version the dry run counted. The daemon matched the client, and auto-update stayed off.
- **The reboot ran through `reboot-chain.sh`**, as written: gate, stop the service, `CHECKPOINT`, stop Postgres, sync, reboot. The persistent journal needed no copy. The app was down **about 19 s**, from its stop to `Application startup complete`.
- **The post-boot probe passed 14 of 14.** No `Persistent=` catch-up ran at boot, and the suite matched its baseline. The re-probe left 0 pending in every apt class.

### What the skill got wrong or lacked

- **`git_origin` misses an SSH host-alias remote** (#391), so a tree's owner reads `unknown`.
- **The profile's fwupd fact is dated too narrowly** (#392): a `may-2026` image has it too.
- **The restarter scan labels `python -m <module>` as a relative script path** (#393). The verdict, `unread`, is right; the reason isn't.
- **No apt mode in `prune-plan.sh`** (#370) still applies: this was the second by-hand fwupd purge.
- **No out-of-cycle window but a knob edit.** An owner taking the monthly run on another day has two choices: commit a window, or pass a copy of the knob with one added (`--config`). The run did the second, and kept the copy in the run directory. The lanes have `origin:<origin>` for a bulletin, but nothing marks a one-off window as one.

### Decisions

- **The backup line stood in for the dump.** Its object was attested by name.
- **Tailscale was followed**, as its own held step, scoped by a tracked pin file.
- **fwupd was purged, not held:** its units had been masked since the image build, and the VM has no firmware.
- **The run was taken out of cycle on the owner's word,** through a knob copy adding `window Thu 13:45-23:30`. The committed knob was left alone.
- **The run's own files were copied out of `/tmp` before the reboot**: the session's scratch lived there, and the boot clears it.

### Surprises

- **An approval arrived after the window closed.** The owner's approval 2 came 50 minutes after Wednesday's window ended, so the run moved. Nothing was started under it.
- **The security set grew by 3 in a day** (curl among them). A dry run older than a few hours undercounts; the 24-hour limit holds, but the count it gives is a floor.
- **A session's scratch is a `/tmp` path**, and the `D` rule clears it at boot. `reboot-chain.sh` listed 116 staged entries, the run's own files among them.

item.title: scan.sh: two gh-failure warnings keep only the last line of gh's stderr
item.body:
Found in the #398 review (CR 327), held there as out of scope. Under #404's boundary rule, this is a child of #404.

**What:** two gh failures in `_scan.py` that become warnings keep only the **last line** of the error:

- `skills/coordinating-epics/scripts/_scan.py:270`: a PR's closing issues unread: `str(e).splitlines()[-1]`
- `skills/coordinating-epics/scripts/_scan.py:504`: a cross-repo ref unreadable: `row["error"] = str(e).splitlines()[-1]`

`Infra`'s message is `"<what>: gh <args> exited N:\n<gh's stderr>"`. So:
- When gh's stderr runs to several lines, only the last one survives. That may be a hint line rather than the cause.
- When gh's stderr is empty, the last line is our own header, `exited N:`, and no cause is kept at all.

**Why:** #398 bound `scan.sh` to the rule that a script never swallows its producer's stderr. These are the two places where the engine keeps only part of it. Unmeasured: I haven't captured a real multi-line gh error on either path. The fake-gh tests (`test_cross_repo_refs_carry_state_or_say_why_not`, `test_a_pr_lookup_failure_is_a_warning`) send one-line errors, so they can't tell the difference.

**Shape:**
- Keep gh's whole stderr in the warning and in `row["error"]`, joined onto one line or kept as is, minus our own header line.
- If the stderr is empty, say so (`gh exited N with no stderr`) rather than echo our header.
- Add a fake-gh test with a two-line error whose cause is on the first line.

item.title: coordinating-epics: scan.sh defaults --ref to origin/HEAD, so a clone without it silently skips the commit cursor (exit 0)
item.body:
## Problem

`scan.sh`'s commit cursor defaults its range tip to `origin/HEAD` (`_scan.py:392`). A clone made without `origin/HEAD` is common: one created with `git init` + `git remote add`, or one whose remote HEAD was never set. In such a clone, the range can't resolve. `commits` comes back `null`, there's one warning, and **the exit code is 0**. A coordinator who reads only the new numbers or the exit code misses that the whole commit cursor didn't run.

Found on the first real adoption of `coordinating-epics` in a consumer repo: CannObserv/address-validator#272, adopted per CannObserv/address-validator#312 on 2026-10-15, with the skill vendored at `fef0611`.

## Repro

```console
$ git rev-parse --verify -q origin/HEAD || echo "origin/HEAD unset"
origin/HEAD unset
$ bash .claude/skills/coordinating-epics/scripts/scan.sh --repo CannObserv/address-validator --epic 272 \
    --since 2026-10-09T22:00:14Z --watermark 310 --from-sha f3c6602
# exit 0; "commits": null; warnings:
#   "commit range not scanned: reading the commit range: git log ... f3c6602..origin/HEAD exited 128:
#    fatal: ambiguous argument 'f3c6602..origin/HEAD': unknown revision or path not in the working tree."
```

With `--ref origin/main`, the same call resolves the range: three commits, the merge attributed to its PR.

**Expected:** a default that works in any clone that has fetched the default branch, or a loud failure when it can't.

## Suggested shape

1. **Resolve the default tip in order:**
   - `git symbolic-ref -q refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`;
   - otherwise `origin/<defaultBranchRef>`, from `gh repo view <repo> --json defaultBranchRef` (one call, and `--repo` is already known);
   - otherwise fail.
2. **When the commit cursor can't run because of the ref** (not a git outage), consider a non-zero exit or a top-level `"commits_skipped": "<reason>"`, so it can't pass as "no commits". The docs already treat a git failure as costing only that cursor. The problem is that this case is a configuration issue, and it recurs on every check-in.
3. **Docs:** one line in `check-in.md` §0, or in the `--ref` help text: "no `origin/HEAD`? pass `--ref origin/<default>` or run `git remote set-head origin -a` once".

## Notes

- The consumer worked around it with `--ref origin/main` and recorded that in its epic's Verify recipe. `git remote set-head origin -a` also fixes it per clone, but every fresh clone would rediscover the problem.
- Related: #404 (coordinating-epics v1.1), if its coordinator wants to slot this. It wasn't filed from one of #404's child reviews, so its boundary rule doesn't make it a child automatically.

item.title: coordinating-epics: scan.sh reads closingIssuesReferences through gh pr view --json, which gh 2.45 lacks, so attribution via a PR's closing links is lost
item.body:
## Problem

`scan.sh` attributes commits to children by asking each PR what it closes: `gh pr view N -R <repo> --json closingIssuesReferences` (`_scan.py:262`). **Ubuntu's apt `gh` 2.45.0 doesn't have that field.** `gh` rejects the field list before doing any lookup, so the call exits 1 for **every** number, issue or PR. The consequences:
- No commit is ever attributed through its PR's closing issues.
- The "not a PR" check (`"Could not resolve to a PullRequest"`) never sees its message, so each issue number in the range adds a warning too.
- Because of #410's last-line truncation, each warning ends in the last field of `gh`'s "Available fields" list, `url`. It reads as `#312's closing issues unread:   url`, which says nothing about the cause.

Found on the first real adoption of `coordinating-epics` in a consumer repo: CannObserv/address-validator#272 (CannObserv/address-validator#312, 2026-10-15), with the skill at `fef0611`.

## Repro (`gh version 2.45.0 (2025-07-18 Ubuntu 2.45.0-1ubuntu0.3)`)

```console
$ gh pr view 313 -R CannObserv/address-validator --json closingIssuesReferences
Unknown JSON field: "closingIssuesReferences"
Available fields:
  additions
  ...
  url
$ echo $?
1
```

`scan.sh` on the same host returned exit 0 with three warnings: `#312's closing issues unread:   url`, the same for #313, and for #311. Two of those are issues and one is a PR.

**Expected:** the closing issues are read on any `gh` the skill supports. Otherwise the scan says plainly that this `gh` is too old for attribution, once per scan, not once per number.

## Suggested shape

- **Read closing issues through GraphQL,** which doesn't depend on the CLI's `--json` field list: `gh api graphql -f query='query($o:String!,$r:String!,$n:Int!){repository(owner:$o,name:$r){pullRequest(number:$n){closingIssuesReferences(first:50){nodes{number url repository{name owner{login}}}}}}}' …`. A `null` `pullRequest` replaces the "Could not resolve to a PullRequest" text match for "this number is an issue".
- **Or check the version up front:** detect the `Unknown JSON field` answer once, emit one warning naming the `gh` version and the floor, and skip attribution for the run.
- **Test:** a fake-gh case that answers `Unknown JSON field` with a multi-line field list. That is also the real multi-line stderr that #410 says it hasn't captured yet.

## Related

- #334 (`using-github-cli`, `gh` ≥ 2.78 floor) describes a different 2.45 break, the `projectCards` field. A floor would cover this one as well, but `scan.sh` shouldn't depend on a floor no hook enforces yet.
- #410: the truncation that hid the cause.
- #404 (coordinating-epics v1.1), if its coordinator wants to slot this. It wasn't filed from one of #404's child reviews.

item.title: coordinating-epics: epic-edit.sh can't reach a section heading or the intro paragraph (rename-section, set-preamble)
item.body:
Child of #404. From CannObserv/processor#24's adoption of v1, finding 145 on #348 ([comment](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/issues/348#issuecomment-6196435243)). The finding's first point, that SKILL.md doesn't say `header` adds only cursor fields, went to #399.

**What:** two kinds of text in an epic body can't be reached by any `epic-edit.sh` op:
- **A section's heading.** `replace-section` replaces the body under a heading and keeps the heading itself; no op renames one.
- **The intro paragraph** above the first section. It holds no ref and sits under no heading, so no op can address it.

**Seen on:**
- CannObserv/processor#24 [stated]: `## Measured state (2026-10-15T15:01Z)` now carries a stale time for good, and its body has to explain that. The intro still calls the protocol "`burning-down-an-epic`, a draft"; the workaround was a protocol note in another section's body.
- #404 [traced]: its Tier 2 heading reads "editor defects this run meets", and it now holds scanner defects too (#406, #407, #410). It can't be renamed without a hand edit, which the Iron Law forbids. Its intro restates the exit criterion, so if the criterion changes, the intro goes stale and can't be fixed through the editor.

**Why it matters:** the Iron Law sends every body edit through `epic-edit.sh`, so text the editor can't reach is frozen. On an adopted epic, that text is often the legacy part that most needs fixing.

**Suggested shape:**
- A `rename-section` op: `{"op": "rename-section", "heading": "old", "to": "new"}`. Same level; refuse a new name that's already a heading (headings are anchors).
- A `set-preamble` op: replace the text between the title (if any) and the cursor list or the first section. Lint it like any changed line, and keep the cursor lines out of its reach.
- In the template: "never put a time in a heading; stamp the bullets" (processor's F133 already stamps bullets).

**Related:** #408 (`replace-section`'s span takes the subsections). Both touch the section ops, so agree on one span model.

item.title: coordinating-epics: scan.sh reads a predictable unattributed commit, the daily submodule bump, at every check-in
item.body:
Child of #404. From CannObserv/processor#24's adoption of v1, finding 146 on #348 ([comment](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/issues/348#issuecomment-6196435243)).

**What:** `scan.sh` attributes each commit in the range. A commit that cites no child or epic and wasn't authored by a bot is `unattributed`, and the coordinator reads it as possible outside work (check-in.md §1). In a repo that vendors skills and runs the refresh hook, a daily `chore: update skills submodules` commit lands in every range. It's correctly `unattributed`, but it's predictable, so reading it becomes a fixed cost at every check-in [stated].

**Why it matters:** a fixed cost gets skimmed. And once in a while the bump matters: on CannObserv/processor#24, `98c5032` also carried the submodule pointer CannObserv/processor#52 needed, so reading it mattered once. A rule that marks the bump as expected has to keep that case visible: the check is that the commit touched only the vendored paths, not just that its subject matches.

**This repo doesn't hit it:** it vendors nothing (`skills-vendor/` doesn't exist) and no submodule bump appears in its recent history [measured]. #404's real use will have to come from a consuming repo's epic, recorded as verification debt there.

**Suggested shape (to weigh):**
- An epic-template line naming the expected unattributed commits, e.g. `- **Expected unattributed:** subject ~ "^chore: update skills submodules$", paths ⊆ skills-vendor/`, read by `scan.sh`. Or a `--expected-unattributed '<subject regex>'` flag with a path filter.
- A matching commit is labelled `expected`, not `unattributed`, only when both the subject and the path set match. A subject match that touched other paths stays `unattributed`, with a warning that says why.
- Test with the fake rig: a bump touching only the vendored path, and one that also touches `src/`.

item.title: coordinating-epics: the ref reader counts a ref quoted in a code span
item.body:
Follow-up to #401 and #402 (CR 330). Found while building them.

**What:** the ref reader has no code-span model. `refs_in` (`_epic_edit.py`) and `_scan.py`'s reads of issue bodies, PR bodies and commit messages call `ref_text`, but they never strip code spans. The lint does strip them, and since #402 it finds spans the CommonMark way. So `` `#7` `` counts as listing #7, though GitHub renders it as code and links nothing [measured: `refs_in` on ``` `` `#7` `` ``` returns this repo's #7].

**Why it matters:** the ref reader feeds four checks: `--account`, the `--scan` mention check, `scan.sh`'s item set and the epic-mention test in `issue_row`. Each counts a ref GitHub doesn't link, and that failure is silent. Take an epic that only quotes an open issue in code: `--account` passes it, but nothing on the page links the issue.

**Suggested fix:** read refs through `outside_code` (with the `tabled` row flag, CR 328) wherever the reader takes text as GitHub renders it. This changes what counts as a mention, so first decide whether a ref quoted in code should count as listing an issue. Then test each reader with a ref inside a double-backtick span.

item.title: test_relative_links: an escaped backtick opens a code span that masks a link
item.body:
Follow-up to #402 (CR 331). Found while building it.

**What:** `tests/structural/test_relative_links.py`'s `_CODE_SPAN_RE` matches equal-length backtick runs, and spans that wrap within a paragraph. It ignores backslash escapes, though. So in `` see \`[x](missing.md)\` here `` it masks `` `[x](missing.md)\` `` as code [measured]. GitHub renders the backticks literally and the link as a link, because an escaped backtick opens no span.

**Why it matters:** a dead link written between escaped backticks is never checked. That is a false negative in a gate, and it is silent.

**Suggested fix:** a backtick run opens a span only when no unescaped backslash comes before it, as `code_spans` in `skills/coordinating-epics/scripts/_epic_edit.py` reads it (#402). Keep the wrap-within-a-paragraph rule this gate already has. Add a test with a dead link between escaped backticks.

item.title: coordinating-epics: REF_PAT misreads a dot before an owner and a non-ASCII letter before #
item.body:
Follow-up to #401 (CR 332). Found while building it. Each case below was measured with `gh api markdown`, in GFM mode with context `gregoryfoster/skills`.

**What:** `REF_PAT` (`_epic_edit.py`) misreads refs in two cases. Both predate #401.

| Text | GitHub | `REF_PAT` |
|---|---|---|
| `v.gregoryfoster/skills#348` | `v.` plus a link to gregoryfoster/skills#348 | the ref `v.gregoryfoster/skills#348`, a repo that doesn't exist |
| `é#5` | `é` plus a link to this repo's #5 | no ref: Python's `\w` matches `é`, so the lookbehind refuses it |

The `.` case misreads because owners can't contain `.`. So GitHub starts the owner after the dot, while `[\w.-]+` takes the dot in.

**Why it matters:** the accounting and the existence check read a different ref from the one GitHub links. Both cases are rare in epic text.

**Suggested fix:** let the owner part match only `[A-Za-z0-9-]`, so a `.` before it is prose. Read the lookbehind's word class as ASCII. Check `BARE_AFTER_QUALIFIED_RE`, `GH_ISSUE_URL_RE` and `SHORT_REF_RE` alongside, since they share the owner pattern. Add the two rows above as tests.

item.title: patching-hosts: the restarter scan treats a relative script path as unreadable instead of resolving it against WorkingDirectory=
item.body:
Found adopting the skill on CannObserv/address-validator (CannObserv/address-validator#311), at `d31a5be`, 2026-10-16.

### Command
```
bash skills/patching-hosts/scripts/probe.sh --config <knob> --refresh-into <scratch>
```

### Output
```
restarters:unread:cache-sweep.service
"cache-sweep.timer runs cache-sweep.service, and the restarter scan can't follow it: cache-sweep.service runs infra/sweep_cache.py, a path relative to its working directory. …"
restarter:address-validator.service
"address-validator.service can restart a service (it may: its OnFailure= target unit-failure@%n.service runs infra/notify_unit_failure.py, a path relative to its working directory), and no restarter line names it …"
```
Three timer services and seven `OnFailure=`-hooked units, all from the same cause. The units:
```
WorkingDirectory=/home/exedev/address-validator
ExecStart=/home/exedev/address-validator/.venv/bin/python infra/sweep_cache.py
```

### Expected
The script read at `WorkingDirectory=` + path (`/home/exedev/address-validator/infra/sweep_cache.py`) and judged one level deep, as an absolute path is. systemd itself resolves a relative interpreter argument against `WorkingDirectory=`, so the file the probe can't find is the one that runs.

### Why
`script_verdict` (probe.sh L2713–2718) returns 2 for any path not starting with `/`, and `unit_restarts` doesn't pass the unit's `WorkingDirectory=` down. Making the paths absolute in the units cleared all ten findings here, but that's a repo change made for the scanner's sake. Resolving the path needs only the unit's `WorkingDirectory=`, which `unit_restarts` already has open. A `~`-prefixed or specifier-bearing directory can stay `unread`.

Related: #393 (the same scan, `python -m`).

item.title: patching-hosts: the restarter scan matches `systemctl start` in a Python docstring, so a notify-only OnFailure= script reads as a restarter
item.body:
Found adopting the skill on CannObserv/address-validator (CannObserv/address-validator#311), at `d31a5be`, 2026-10-16.

### Command
```
bash skills/patching-hosts/scripts/probe.sh   # after making the OnFailure= target's script path absolute
```

### Output
The `OnFailure=` notifier `infra/notify_unit_failure.py` is read as a restarter. The one line matching `RESTART_RE` is in its module docstring:
```
Set by systemd (>= 251) for an ``OnFailure=`` handler; absent on a manual
``systemctl start unit-failure@<unit>.service``:
```

### Expected
A docstring describing how the script is invoked doesn't make it a restarter. #351 says one that only notifies isn't one, and this one only notifies.

### Why
`script_verdict` (probe.sh L2728) drops only lines starting with `#` before matching `RESTART_RE` (L2666), so Python docstrings, string literals and help text all count. Rewording the docstring cleared it here, but the next repo to adopt the skill hits the same thing in a usage line. Options:
- for Python, match only a call shape (`subprocess…systemctl`, `"systemctl"` in an argv list), or skip triple-quoted blocks;
- or report the matching line number in the finding, so the owner can tell a docstring from a call and declare `not-restarter:` (which needs #420 for `OnFailure=` targets).

Related: #418 (relative paths), #420.

item.title: patching-hosts: an unreadable OnFailure= target has no `not-restarter:` exception, unlike a timer's service
item.body:
Found adopting the skill on CannObserv/address-validator (CannObserv/address-validator#311), at `d31a5be`, 2026-10-16.

### Command
```
bash skills/patching-hosts/scripts/probe.sh --config <knob> --refresh-into <scratch>
```

### Output
```
{"severity":"knob","id":"restarter:address-validator.service","exception_what":null,
 "message":"address-validator.service can restart a service (it may: its OnFailure= target unit-failure@%n.service runs infra/notify_unit_failure.py, a path relative to its working directory), and no restarter line names it or its timer, …"}
```
Seven of these, one per unit hooked to the same notify-only `unit-failure@.service`.

### Expected
The same choice a timer's unreadable service gets: declare `restarter <unit>`, **or** `exception not-restarter:<target> <review-by> <reason>`.

### Why
In `read_restarters` (probe.sh ~L2876), `onfailure_restarts` returning 2 (couldn't read) adds the unit to `found` as a restarter. Its finding carries `exception_what: null`, while an unreadable timer service gets `restarters:unread:` with `not-restarter:<svc>` (L2909–2912). So with an `OnFailure=` target the scan can't read, the owner can only:
- declare the notifier a `restarter`, which #351 says stops the watched service around every held step; or
- change the unit until the scan can read it.

One `not-restarter:unit-failure@.service` (keyed by the target, or its template) would cover every unit hooked to it.

Related: #419 (a docstring read as a restart), #418.

item.title: patching-hosts knob: `window` can't express a week of the month ("2nd Sunday") for the monthly `scheduled` posture
item.body:
Found adopting the skill on CannObserv/address-validator (CannObserv/address-validator#311), at `d31a5be`, 2026-10-16.

### Command
The owner's window is **monthly, 2nd Sunday, 17:00–19:00 UTC**. The closest knob line is
```
window Sun 17:00-19:00
```
`read-knob.sh` accepts it.

### Expected
Some way to say "the 2nd Sunday". `scheduled` is a monthly posture (policy.md), but `window` takes only a weekday, so this line lets `apply.sh` run on any Sunday. Something like:
```
window Sun#2 17:00-19:00          # systemd.time(7)'s day-of-month range: Sun *-*-08..14
```
or a `cadence monthly-nth 2` line beside the weekday.

### Why
`window <weekday> <HH:MM-HH:MM>` (knob.md; _knob-lib.sh L170, L496). The gate checks that a step's span falls inside a window, but not which week of the month it is in. Here the repo's test pins the line, and the 2nd-Sunday rule lives only in a comment and the operator's calendar.

item.title: patching-hosts: a uv with no `audit` subcommand (exeuntu Feb-2026's 0.10.4) leaves the language class unaudited with only "exited 2"
item.body:
Found adopting the skill on CannObserv/address-validator (CannObserv/address-validator#311), at `d31a5be`, 2026-10-16.

### Command
```
bash skills/patching-hosts/scripts/probe.sh --config <knob> --refresh-into <scratch>
```

### Output
```
"pending": {"language": {"trees": [{"lockfile": "uv.lock", "audited": false,
  "why": "uv audit exited 2: error: unrecognized subcommand 'audit'"}], "complete": false}}
```
The host's uv is `/usr/local/bin/uv` 0.10.4, from the exe.dev Feb-2026 image. On a copy of the same `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock`, `uvx --from uv uv audit --frozen` (uv 0.13.1) found **78 advisory entries in 15 packages**.

### Expected
- The finding names the cause: "uv 0.10.4 has no `audit` (needs ≥ <first version with it>)". Not a raw exit code.
- It goes to the right owner: `/usr/local/bin/uv` is image-shipped, so the image owner (or an `owner` line).
- readings.md gives the fallback that worked here: a newer uv from the user's cache, run on the copy the probe already makes. Or the probe tries `uvx --from 'uv>=<min>' uv audit` itself under `--refresh-into`, which already allows network access.

### Why
probe.sh L1775–1790 takes the first uv it finds and runs `audit --frozen`. It reads exit 2 as a generic failure (L1829), so the sixth class reads "not audited" with no next step, on every host from that image.

item.title: patching-hosts: every `health` line runs at every probe, so a recovery check (real requests, new rows) can't be scoped to data-store steps
item.body:
Found adopting the skill on CannObserv/address-validator (CannObserv/address-validator#311), at `d31a5be`, 2026-10-16.

### Setup
run.md asks a data-store step to prove recovery, not liveness: a real request, a new row, and a cache hit on the repeat. The place for that is a `health` line. Here it's a script that checks Postgres is ready, sends `POST /api/v2/validate` twice, and needs both rows in `audit_log` plus a cache hit on the second.

### What happens
`probe.sh` runs **every** `health` line pre-run (`read_health pre-run`, L3127), including a plain read-only probe. So each probe:
- makes two real API calls on the production service;
- writes two audit rows;
- reads the production DB;
- and, on a cache miss, spends provider quota.

An operator who wants a read-only reading, or a session that may not touch prod data, has to strip the line from a copy of the knob and pass `--config`, as we did here.

Even the plain liveness line writes: this app audits `/api/v2/health` too.

### Expected
Some way to separate the two kinds of check, for example:
```
health curl -sf http://localhost:8000/api/v2/health      # every reading
recovery <command>                                       # held data-store steps and --post-boot only
```
or a `health --steps <step>…` qualifier. Alternatively, readings.md could say plainly that a health line runs at every probe, so it must be safe to run anytime and cheap.

### Why
readings.md's health baseline needs every check green before a run. But a recovery check is only meaningful around a data-store restart, and it has side effects, which liveness checks don't.

item.title: coordinating-epics scan.sh: default --ref origin/HEAD fails when unset; old gh turns every closingIssuesReferences read into 'unread: url'
item.body:
Found while adopting `coordinating-epics` v1 (`fef0611`) for CannObserv/usa-wa#414 (CannObserv/usa-wa#500), across the 2026-10-15 and 10-16 check-ins. Two problems in `scripts/scan.sh` (`_scan.py`), both reproduced on the usa-wa host: Ubuntu, gh 2.45.0 from apt, a prod checkout cloned long ago.

## 1. The default `--ref origin/HEAD` fails when the remote's HEAD ref is unset

```
$ bash scan.sh --repo CannObserv/usa-wa --epic 414 --since … --watermark 497 --from-sha 65e9a7b
warnings: commit range not scanned: … git log --format=… 65e9a7b..origin/HEAD exited 128:
fatal: ambiguous argument '65e9a7b..origin/HEAD': unknown revision or path not in the working tree.
```

`refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` exists only when the checkout was made by `git clone`, or after `git remote set-head origin -a`. Here it's unset, so the commit range, and with it the per-commit child attribution, is silently skipped unless every call passes `--ref origin/main`. The warning says so, but the coordinator has to notice it on every check-in.

**Expected:** when `origin/HEAD` doesn't resolve, fall back to the remote's default branch. `gh repo view --json defaultBranchRef` gives it, as `origin/<name>`. Or fail loudly instead of returning `"commits": null` beside an otherwise complete report.

## 2. gh < (the version that added the field) makes every PR's closing issues "unread: url"

```
warnings: ["#497's closing issues unread:   url", "#498's closing issues unread:   url", "#434's closing issues unread:   url", "#430's closing issues unread:   url"]
```

`pr_closes()` calls `gh pr view N --json closingIssuesReferences`. gh 2.45.0 doesn't know the field:

```
$ gh pr view 498 -R CannObserv/usa-wa --json closingIssuesReferences
Unknown JSON field: "closingIssuesReferences"
Available fields:
  additions
  …
  url
```

The warning keeps only the error's last line, which is the last entry in gh's field list (`url`), so it reads as a URL problem. The same failure also hits plain issues (#434, #430), because only "Could not resolve to a PullRequest" is treated as "not a PR". Attribution then falls back to subject refs, which happened to work here because every commit subject carried its issue number.

**Expected, any of:**
- read `closingIssuesReferences` through `gh api graphql`, which doesn't depend on the gh CLI version;
- declare a minimum gh version under the skill's `compatibility:` and check it once at startup;
- at least, report the whole error, or recognise "Unknown JSON field" and say "gh too old for closingIssuesReferences".

Ubuntu 24.04's apt gh is 2.45.0, so other hosts in the cohort may be on it too.

item.title: New skill: managing-host-disk — adopt Provisioner's canonical disk GC + headroom sensor, plus the repo-side knobs (cohort-wide)
item.body:
## Why
Root-disk exhaustion keeps recurring across the CannObserv cohort, and six hosts have each built their own GC (inventory and comparison in **CannObserv/provisioner#61**). That issue proposes **one canonical host-tooling GC + headroom sensor, owned by Provisioner and shipped in co-image-base.**

The image only reaches new or migrated VMs. Every other host needs a way to adopt the same files now, and every repo has disk costs of its own that a host-level tool shouldn't guess at. That's a skill's job.

## Proposed skill: `managing-host-disk` (name open)
1. **Adopt the canonical GC.**
   - On a host not yet on co-image-base, install the provisioner#61 script, unit, timer and journald drop-in from Provisioner's repo at a pinned commit. It is never a fork, so there's one source.
   - Retire the host's own implementation in the same change: wslcb `disk_hygiene.py`, address-validator `disk-hygiene.sh`, watcher `cleanup.sh`, observo's cache timers, usa-wa `disk-gc.sh`, power-map `prune_disk.py`.
2. **Wire the headroom sensor.** Request a co-status dead-man monitor through the provider repo (the CannObserv/status#48 shape: name, interval, grace, renotify, `enabled: false` until the first `ok`). Then rehearse a `--test` alert end to end.
3. **Repo-side knobs** the host tool must not own, each a measured, per-repo decision:
   - **pytest basetemps:** `tmp_path_retention_count = 1` + `tmp_path_retention_policy = "failed"`. Before this, pytest kept 3 runs of ~480M each on power-map. Note that pytest prunes at *exit*, so a failing run's residue survives green runs (CannObserv/power-map#665).
   - **Worktree cost:** each worktree's own `.venv` + `node_modules` (~0.2–0.8G), and pruning orphaned worktree dirs.
   - **App data tiers:** retention contracts, never automatic (cf. CannObserv/usa-wa#396).
4. **Pitfalls to encode** (each found on one host, probably present on others):
   - a bare `uv cache prune` blocks for good on a long-running `uv run`; use `--force`;
   - liveness-only pruning deletes an install in progress, so add a grace window (usa-wa#394, power-map#669);
   - `extensions/` must be a GC root (usa-wa#399);
   - keep the pinned SocratiCode npx tree by `sha512(spec)[:16]`, for both the declared and the launched spec (usa-wa#485);
   - identify in-use paths from `/proc` exe/cwd/maps/fd, **never from process args**, since a session's shell argv carries `GH_TOKEN`.

## Related
- #390 (patching-hosts free-space checks), which should read the same sensor.
- The `init-socraticode` pin work (#295/#327/#332), which defines which npx tree is pinned.

item.title: coordinating-epics: epic-edit.sh's exit-3 message keeps only the last line of a failed PATCH's error
item.body:
Found in the review of #406, #410 and #411 (CR 350), and held there as out of scope: #410's spec is the two warnings in `_scan.py`. Under #404's boundary rule, this is a child of #404, for its coordinator to slot.

**What:** `epic-edit.sh` sums up a failed PATCH by the last line of its error, in two places that both return exit 3 (read-back unconfirmed). Line numbers are at 3cea77a:

- `skills/coordinating-epics/scripts/_epic_edit.py:1611`: the PATCH failed, and reading the body back failed too.
- `skills/coordinating-epics/scripts/_epic_edit.py:1639`: the PATCH failed, and the body now matches neither the one sent nor the one before.

Both use `head=f"the PATCH failed ({str(patch_error).splitlines()[-1]}), and"`. On these two paths `patch_error` isn't printed anywhere else. On the third path, where the PATCH landed anyway, the full error is printed as a `WARNING`.

**Why it matters:** this is #410's defect, in the editor. `Infra`'s message is `"<what>: gh <args> exited N:\n<gh's stderr>"`:
- When gh's stderr runs to several lines, only the last one survives, and that may be a hint line rather than the cause.
- When gh's stderr is empty, what's left is our own `… exited N:` header.

Exit 3 is the case where the operator has to work out by hand whether the write landed, so the cause matters most here.

**Shape:**
- Once #410's branch lands, `gh()` attaches gh's stderr and exit code to the `Infra` it raises (`e.stderr`, `e.code`), and `_scan.py` gains `gh_cause(e)`. That returns gh's whole stderr without our header, or `gh exited N with no stderr`.
- Move `gh_cause` into `_epic_edit.py` beside `Infra`, which `_scan.py` already imports from, and use it at both sites.
- If a one-line `head` is wanted, put the whole cause after it instead.
- Test: the rig's `patch_fails_after_apply` sends a one-line `HTTP 502: Bad Gateway`, so it can't tell the difference. Add a multi-line PATCH error whose cause is on the first line, and an empty one, on both exit-3 paths.

Unmeasured: I haven't seen a real multi-line PATCH error. The shape is the one #410 measured, gh's `Unknown JSON field` answer.

item.title: patching-hosts: an owner line never matches a container image, so the knob can't declare who updates one
item.body:
Found on co-index (CannObserv/index#11). Skill at `f476af8`.

## What happened

co-index runs Ollama from an image this repo builds: `socraticode/ollama-slim:<version>`, from a pinned `ollama/ollama` base. A new engine can change every stored embedding with the model unchanged, which is what CannObserv/index#11 is about. So the image's update belongs to the repo and never to a patching run. knob.md's `owner` directive says it covers "a component apt doesn't reach", and policy.md says "the repo that installed a component owns it (a pinned tool, a container image)". So the knob declares:

```
owner socraticode/ollama-slim self
```

`read-knob.sh` parses it with no finding:

```
$ bash read-knob.sh --host co-index | jq -c '.owner, .findings'
[{"component":"socraticode/ollama-slim","repo":"self","line":25}]
[]
```

The probe never applies it to the image. `read_outside_apt` matches `KNOB_OWNER` globs against the paths of binaries under `/usr/local/bin` and `~/.local/bin` only. The container-image loop records `image` and `created`, and no owner:

```
$ bash probe.sh | jq -c '.. | .container_images? // empty'
[{"image":"socraticode/ollama-slim:0.34.0","created":"3 hours ago"},{"image":"socraticode/ollama-slim:latest","created":"5 weeks ago"},{"image":"qdrant/qdrant:v1.17.0","created":"7 months ago"}]
```

So the image is reported as unowned (CannObserv/index#9 recorded it as "outside apt, not assessed"), and the knob line does nothing.

## Expected

An `owner` glob matched against each container image's `repository:tag` (`socraticode/ollama-slim` matching every tag, as a binary's glob matches its basename), and the image entry carrying `owner` and `owner_line` as a binary's does. An `owner` line that matches nothing on the host might also be a finding: a line that silently does nothing is how this went unnoticed.

item.title: coordinating-epics: process-log entry — 2026-10-17 private-release-move
item.body:
A process-log entry for `coordinating-epics`, from a run on a host that consumes this repo as a submodule. The process-log rules send it here as an issue, because writing it in the vendored copy would leave the host with a modified submodule. The host repo is private, so the entry is anonymized as `private-release-move`.

**Please add** the entry below as `process-log/2026/2026-10-17-private-release-move.md`, and its row to `process-log/2026/index.md`.

**New candidates for #404:**
- **Finding 4:** `epic-edit.sh` can't edit a sub-bullet under a child's line.
- **Finding 8:** kickoff prompts should require fixing the review before reporting.

Findings 3 and 5 are second sightings of #411/#424 and #399; no new issue is needed for them.

---

## Session 2026-10-17 — private-release-move

**Shape:** design-doc epic. Six children, serial, operator-paced. A single-host FastAPI service moved from "systemd runs the dev checkout" to a root-owned release run by a dedicated system user, with root-only secrets. Ran 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-17: seven check-ins, closed on an empty re-scan.

**Skill coverage:** the coordinator ran check-ins 1–6 by hand and adopted the skill only at close-out (`--adopt-live` on the final write). The findings below include what the skill would have caught earlier.

### Findings
1. **A box ticked by someone else turned up at every check-in.** Implementer threads, or the operator, ticked the child's box before the coordinator verified it, on 5 of 6 children. A hand-run coordinator just kept the tick. `epic-edit.sh`'s foreign-tick check is the right default, and this run is evidence for it.
2. **Independent verification found what the reports left out,** four times:
   - **Design:** a measured cgroup escape. Memory-capped children launched with `systemd-run --user --scope` sat outside the service's `MemoryMax`. It became its own child.
   - **A child's side note** had a 46-hour outage of a third-party credential that the health probe never saw. The journal showed onset and recovery, and an issue was filed.
   - **A cleaned path reappeared.** By bisecting test files with a throwaway teardown hook, the coordinator traced it to a test factory default, not production.
   - **A behaviour change nobody stated:** once the service's working directory moved to the release, a relative `env_file` entry stopped resolving. The dev env file then no longer reached production in any form, and the docs had to say so.

   Rule support: "verify live, never from the report".
3. **`scan.sh` failed its commit range when `origin/HEAD` was unset** in the local clone (`fatal: ambiguous argument … origin/HEAD`). It succeeded with `--ref origin/main`. The same run printed `closing issues unread: url` for every closing-issues read, on gh 2.45. **Already filed and closed upstream** as #411 and #424; this host's vendored copy predates the fixes. It is a second sighting, so no new issue.
4. **`epic-edit.sh` can't reach a sub-bullet under a ref's line.** A stale "Open: backup run due …" sub-bullet needed a `replace-section` of the whole checklist. (Related: #408, `replace-section`'s reach over `###` subsections.) **Tool gap, not yet filed:** a `set-subline` op, or `note` with `replace_sub`.
5. **A legacy bold-paragraph cursor** (`**Last check-in:** …`, not a list item) was rewritten in place by `header`, while the new cursors went into a separate list. The result has mixed formats. A second sighting of **#399**.
6. **The agent permission classifier blocked prod-touching verification in child threads:** creating a short prod Job, and a read-only prod-DB column scan. Both went through only with the operator's per-run consent. **Brief rule:** a Verify step that needs a prod Job or a prod-DB read names the operator's consent as a precondition, in the brief.
7. **A gate dated after the last child held the epic open about 19 hours:** a nightly backup timer after the user switch. That was acceptable here because it was short and certain. close-out.md's "a check dated after the end goes to a dated issue" (watcher F60) would have closed sooner. Record the choice either way.
8. **Kickoff prompts should say "fix the review", not "run the review"** (operator's revision). Implementer threads sometimes reported before their review's fixes had landed:
   - On one child, 12 review findings in 3 rounds landed after its closing comment.
   - On another, a doc fix held in review shipped after its first Verify report.

   Each time, the SHA the coordinator verified was no longer the final one. **Rule for hand-off.md's kickoff prompt and the implementer contract:** run the code review and **fix its findings**, or record each declined one with its reason, before reporting. The report then names the final SHA, the one the coordinator verifies.

### Index row
| [2026-10-17](2026-10-17-private-release-move.md) | private-release-move | design-doc epic, 6 children, 7 check-ins | Foreign ticks on 5/6 children; independent checks found 4 unstated facts (cgroup escape, unseen 46 h outage, test leak, env-file cwd); `epic-edit.sh` can't edit sub-bullets; Verify steps needing prod Jobs/DB reads need consent named in the brief; kickoffs should say "fix the review" before reporting |

item.title: coordinating-epics: no epic-edit.sh op reaches a sub-bullet under a child's line
item.body:
Child of #404. From a private run's process-log entry, #428 (finding 4), filed on the operator's word, 2026-10-17.

**What:** no `epic-edit.sh` op reaches a sub-bullet under a child's line. `find_ref_line` (`_epic_edit.py:463`) finds a line only by the ref that leads it (`line_ref`). A sub-bullet such as `  - Open: backup run due …` under `- [ ] #12 …` leads with no ref, so `set-line`, `note` and `tick` can't address it [traced at 9851de0]. `add-line` places new lines after a ref's block (CR 250), but it can't change or remove one that's there.

**Seen on:** the private run in #428 [stated]. A stale "Open: …" sub-bullet under a child needed a `replace-section` of the whole checklist to change one line. That put every child's line at risk to fix one note, the same blast radius #408 describes for `replace-section`.

**Why it matters:** sub-bullets are where runs keep a child's open items, residuals and dated deferrals. The template's own notes are inline, but adopted epics often hold them as sub-bullets. Once written, they're frozen short of a whole-section rewrite, which the Iron Law makes the only way.

**Suggested shape (to weigh):**
- A `set-subline` op: `{"op": "set-subline", "ref": "#12", "match": "Open: backup", "line": "  - Done: backup ran 2026-10-17"}`. It addresses the one sub-bullet under #12's line whose text starts with `match`, and refuses on zero or several matches. `"line": ""` removes it.
- Or a `note` variant with `replace_sub`, as #428 suggests.
- Lint the new sub-line like any changed line, and keep the derived counts right if a sub-bullet holds a box.

**Related:** #408 and #413 (the section ops' reach). The three should agree on what a "block" under a heading or a ref is.

criteria.out of epic: Not this epic's work: another skill, service, area or epic, a record or notice with no action, or tooling around the epic rather than its work. It is said so plainly and cross-linked only where it changes a remaining step.

criteria.park: This epic's concern, but not to be done yet: it waits on a trigger (another repo, a decision, a date, an event) and goes in the parked table with that trigger.

item.title: coordinating-epics: the kickoff prompt and implementer contract should require fixing the review's findings before reporting
item.body:
Child of #404. From a private run's process-log entry, #428 (finding 8, the operator's own revision there), filed on the operator's word, 2026-10-17.

**What:** the kickoff prompt (`references/hand-off.md:45-55`, the text block) says "Run the review, report, and pause before shipping". SKILL.md's implementer contract (`SKILL.md:114-120`) lists no review step at all. Neither says the review's findings must be **fixed** before the report.

**Why it matters:** in the private run, implementer threads reported before their review's fixes had landed [stated, #428]:
- on one child, 12 review findings in 3 rounds landed after its closing comment;
- on another, a doc fix held in review shipped after its first Verify report.

Each time, the SHA the coordinator verified was no longer the final one. That breaks check-in.md §1's unit of verification, the commit range, without anything noticing.

On #404 the operator adopted the wording from 2026-10-17 on, in the kickoff prompts this coordinator writes. #404's earlier children happened to land their review fixes before closing (each closing comment lists its CR rounds). So the risk is real where a thread stops at "run".

**Suggested shape:**
- hand-off.md's kickoff prompt: "Run the code review and fix its findings, or record each declined one with its reason, before you report. The report names the final SHA."
- SKILL.md's implementer contract: the same as one bullet. SKILL.md is held to 6,000 tokens and sits at about 4,313 (estimate).
- check-in.md §1: a child whose closing comment predates commits in its range is verified on the range's tip, not the reported SHA. That is already the rule; one sentence ties it to this case.

item.title: coordinating-epics process log: close out the 2026-10-13 private-backlog run (adopted mid-run; findings 155–159)
item.body:
The private-backlog run (`references/process-log/2026/2026-10-13-private-backlog.md`) was still open when its entry was written. It closed on **2026-10-17**. This asks for that entry, and its index row, to be updated with the close-out below. The host repo is private, so this names mechanisms only. The skill is vendored there, so the entry isn't edited in place.

### Shape at close
- **Check-ins:** 25, from 2026-10-05 to 2026-10-17 (13 days from creation).
- **Way out:** the exit criterion was met with about 30 hardening items still open. The operator chose "close now, file the rest". The unticked lines left the epic as ordinary open issues, and parked items kept their label and triggers. The accounting check (`--account`) passed with every open issue referenced. The dated and external checks moved to one watch issue.
- **The last stretch:** a design issue (move production off the development checkout) grew into a six-child sub-epic, coordinated by its implementing thread with its own check-ins. Its step 0, an environment-file leak, shipped ahead of the design. The parent epic tracked it as one line until its last gate (a nightly scheduled run) passed.
- **The skill was adopted mid-run, at check-in 23,** through "Adopt an epic that exists": one `--adopt-live` write after a scan with one-time cursors. Check-ins 23–25 ran on `scan.sh` and `epic-edit.sh`.

### What the scripts caught or missed after adoption
- **Caught:** a foreign tick by an implementing thread (refused until `--accept-ticks`); legacy short cross-repo refs, including slash-joined forms, on every touched line; and a new issue missing from the body (the re-scan after filing).
- **Missed, host-side:** the clone had no `origin/HEAD`, so `scan.sh`'s commit cursor was skipped with only a warning until `--ref origin/main` was passed. Consider making a missing `origin/HEAD` a hard error, or falling back to the remote's default branch.
- **Friction:** the editor appends to the Log, so a newest-first log had to be reordered once, through `replace-section`, which lints every line it touches.

### Findings (numbered on from 154)

155. **A brief's recommended fix can be capped by a constraint outside the files it names.** To stop duplicate audit rows on replay, the brief offered "derive the timestamp deterministically from the message id" and warned about two hazards in the existing helper. The implementer found a third: the database's unique key also includes the emitter's identity, and that changes when a process restarts or a sibling shard takes over. So the deterministic scheme dedups only under the same emitter, and the headline case stays uncovered. The coverage statement in its closing comment then claimed the stage was single-consumer, and a review round corrected it after closure, because the stage registry marks it shardable. Two lessons. First, when a brief proposes an idempotency scheme, it should name the **whole** dedup key, read from the schema, not only the field being changed. Second, a closing comment's claims about the system's shape ("single consumer", "startup-only reclaim") should be checked against the registry that defines that shape before the item closes.

156. **Re-measure a "production is unaffected" claim per item, not for the headline item.** An issue filed by a review said a bad seed migration left nothing in production. That was true for the one key the review cared about. A one-line query at hand-off showed the other three seeded keys **were** in production, unread since they were seeded. That turned "a fresh-install fix" into "a production data change": confirm there are no readers, apply it deliberately in a quiet window, and record the counts before and after. When an issue's claim covers several things, the coordinator should measure each of them before the brief repeats the claim.

157. **Don't let a large design hold a cheap mitigation hostage.** The last queued item was a design issue: move the service off the development checkout, with root-only secrets. Re-reading it at hand-off, the coordinator found the exposure it described had grown. The development environment file loaded into production held six times as many credentials as when the issue was filed, several of them write-capable, and every child process parsing untrusted input inherited them. It also held nothing production needed, so dropping one line from the service unit was close to risk-free. The coordinator asked the operator whether to do that now, as step 0 of the design thread, rather than wait for the design's approval and implementation. They said yes. When a design issue's problem statement includes a live exposure, check at hand-off whether some slice of it can be closed cheaply ahead of the design, and offer that slice separately.

158. **A sibling thread can write the coordinator's baseline, which blinds the foreign-edit check.** The coordinator detected foreign edits by diffing the live body against a baseline copy saved in a durable per-user state directory. An implementing thread running a sub-epic learned the same procedure, perhaps from shared host memory. It edited the parent epic's body (a correct rewrite of one standing check) and then saved its own result into the coordinator's baseline file. The next check-in's diff came back clean while the live body carried an edit the coordinator hadn't made. The coordinator caught it only because a closing comment claimed that edit and the coordinator went looking. The issue's edit history (who, when) confirmed it. Two fixes. The coordinator should read the body's edit history at each check-in, not only diff it against a local copy. And the baseline should live where only the coordinator's tool writes, under a guarded editor, rather than as a plain file other threads can copy.

159. **Adopting the packaged skill mid-run cost one check-in's write and surfaced three snags.** The adoption followed the skill's own "adopt an epic that exists" path: one guarded call with `--adopt-live`, preceded by a scan with one-time cursors. Three things needed attention. The clone had no `origin/HEAD`, so the commit range was silently skipped until `--ref` was passed. Lint refused legacy short cross-repo refs on every line the call touched, including slash-joined forms. And the editor appends to the Log, so a newest-first log had to be reordered once in the same call. None of these blocked the adoption, but each would trip a later check-in that didn't know about it, so they belong in the adopting repo's notes.

item.title: patching-hosts profile: a tailscaled upgrade cut the tailnet for ~2 s; tailnet listeners and connections survived (co-provisioner, 1.102.4 → 1.104.1)
item.body:
## From co-provisioner, 2026-10-17: what a `tailscaled` upgrade costs, measured once

Filed from CannObserv/provisioner#60, where `co-provisioner` was upgraded from Tailscale 1.102.4 to 1.104.1, upstream exeuntu's new floor. **It was a hand run, outside `apply.sh`** (the owner's decision; the knob is CannObserv/provisioner#67).
- **Host:** `co-provisioner`, co-image-base `:c70ae45`, on exeuntu `main-1b74aab`.
- **Run:** `sudo NEEDRESTART_MODE=l apt-get install --only-upgrade tailscale=1.104.1`, at 2026-10-17T14:17:25Z.

Everything here is [measured] unless tagged. It's one host and one run.

### 1. The tailnet gap, and what survived it [profile]

The profile's Tailscale section says "Upgrading tailscaled drops the host's tailnet path, so it waits for a planned window". That's true. Here's how far it dropped:

- **Gap ≈ 2.0 s.** `tailscaled got signal terminated; shutting down` at 14:17:30.385. Then a `--cleanup` pass, then `Program starting: v1.104.1` at 14:17:31.091, and `Switching ipn state Starting -> Running` at 14:17:32.374. TUN mode. `tailscale0` was removed and recreated: the new daemon logged `failed to look up link "tailscale0": Link not found` during cleanup.
- **Listeners bound to the tailnet address survived.** Two uvicorn APIs bind `100.105.197.95:9000` and `:9001` and nothing else. They kept their PIDs and their sockets, with no restart. Both answered `/ready` 200 at 14:17:41, the first probe after the restart.
- **An established tailnet TCP connection survived.** It was a Redis client on `100.105.197.95:60846`, connected to a peer's `:6379`. It stayed established on the same 4-tuple, and the client kept reading with no reconnect and no log line. Its per-minute heartbeat landed at 14:16:50, 14:17:54 and 14:18:54.
- **systemd tied nothing to `tailscaled`:** the units have `After=tailscaled.service` only, with no `BindsTo=` or `PartOf=`. So the survival is the kernel's and the applications', not a dependency being restarted.

**Proposed note** for the Tailscale section, after "drops the host's tailnet path":

> On co-provisioner (1.102.4 → 1.104.1, TUN mode, 2026-10-17), the drop was ≈2 s. Listeners bound to the tailnet address, and an established tailnet TCP connection, survived in place without a restart. Whether a host's own services ride it out is the host's to confirm in its run (CannObserv/provisioner#60).

### 2. `tailscale` restarts its own daemon [profile]

A row for "Packages that restart their own services":

| Package | Behaviour | Hosts |
|---|---|---|
| `tailscale` | restarts `tailscaled` from its postinst (`deb-systemd-invoke restart 'tailscaled.service'`), whatever needrestart's mode | co-provisioner |

needrestart (3.6-7ubuntu4.5, `NEEDRESTART_MODE=l`) reported "No services need to be restarted" after the restart had already happened. The `Daemon:` line from `tailscale version --daemon` then matched `Client:` (`1.104.1-t7f4efe814-g8da26756c`), which is the profile's done-check.

### 3. A newer daemon's start, without a boot, didn't re-apply auto-update [profile, no answer]

The profile leaves this open, from replicator#131 and #357: "Whether the boot or the newer daemon triggered it is unmeasured". Here, the newer daemon started with no boot:
- it logged no `using tailnet default auto-update setting` line;
- its prefs read `update=check`;
- `AutoUpdate` stayed `{Check: true, Apply: false}`.

**This doesn't answer it.** The tailnet's auto-update default is **off** [stated, the owner, from the admin console, 2026-10-18]. A daemon that re-applied the default would have applied off, so the result can't tell the two cases apart. The setting for this device in the console wasn't confirmed. The node's own prefs, read on the host, were `Apply: false` before and after.

**A question for the profile:** co-replicator logged `using tailnet default auto-update setting: true` on 2026-10-06 (replicator#131). If both hosts are on the same tailnet, either the default changed after that date, or that line doesn't report the tailnet-wide default. Not checked.

### Also, the journal

PID 1 wrote **0** lines across the restart. That's CannObserv/provisioner#62: exeuntu's `LogTarget=console` stops PID 1's journal lines after the first daemon-reload. `systemctl show tailscaled -p MainPID,ActiveEnterTimestamp` was the proof of the restart. A run that looks for systemd's `Stopping`/`Started` lines on such a host finds none.

item.title: curating-context: no warrant shape for linking a doc in another repo from an index line (the cohort charter's ask)
item.body:
From a curating-context run on CannObserv/replicator, curating-context `version: "1.31"`, vendored at `9851de0`, `prove-no-loss.sh` identical to `fb6c297` (CannObserv/replicator#137, PR CannObserv/replicator#143).

## What happens
cannobserv's cohort charter (CannObserv/cannobserv `docs/BOUNDARIES.md`, cannobserv#562) asks **each sibling repo to link it from its own AGENTS.md**. For replicator, the natural edit was to extend the existing index line for the charter's annex:

```
- [replicator-boundaries.md](docs/contracts/replicator-boundaries.md) — what Replicator may become; run its three tests against any proposed capability
+ - [replicator-boundaries.md](docs/contracts/replicator-boundaries.md) — what Replicator may become, annex to cannobserv's [charter](https://github.com/CannObserv/cannobserv/blob/main/docs/BOUNDARIES.md); run its three tests against any proposed capability
```

That keeps every word and atom of the old line and adds one link. `prove-no-loss.sh` refuses the `index` entry:

```
the line that keeps it adds no link to a doc AGENTS.md did not link at --base
```

This is by design. `link_path()` returns `None` for any URL ("a URL … names no file here"), so a cross-repo doc can never be in `unindexed_docs`. None of the other warrants fits either. `tighten` would be false, because the line grew, and `retarget` and `duplicate` don't apply.

## What we did
We kept the old line verbatim and added the link as its **own** line, nested so that "its" has one referent:

```
- [replicator-boundaries.md](docs/contracts/replicator-boundaries.md) — what Replicator may become; run its three tests against any proposed capability
  - [cohort charter](https://github.com/CannObserv/cannobserv/blob/main/docs/BOUNDARIES.md) — its parent
```

A new line loses nothing, so it needs no warrant. The cost was measured exactly: about 16 tokens for the bare line, against about 33 for the same URL inside a reworded line.

## Why it will recur
- The charter's ask goes to **every** cohort sibling (archiver, watcher, notifier, broker, observo). Each will reach the same refusal if it extends a line in place.
- Most of these AGENTS.md files sit near the 6000 budget, so each one is tempted to extend a line rather than add one.

## Suggestions (either would do)
1. **Document the shape.** In `--help` under "The index warrant", and in Phase 5 step 3: a link to a doc in **another repo** is added as its own line (nested under the line it relates to if that helps), not by extending a line. `index` deliberately doesn't cover URLs.
2. **Or admit declared external docs.** Let a committed knob, say `.skills/context-external-docs` with one URL per line, make those URLs eligible for `index`. The rest of the check stays as it is: every word and atom kept, only the new link added.

Related: #282 (`index` itself), #338 point 2 (rewording an index description).
