item.title: patching-hosts: a Redis whose redis.conf has a `user` line is refused as "its aclfile sets the users", and only at the recovery point, never by the probe
item.body:
Found in host 6's first monthly run under the scripts (process log `2026-09-28-host-6.md`; a private repo, so no identifiers here), at `468bf14`, on 2026-10-20. It follows #379.

### Command
```
bash skills/patching-hosts/scripts/recovery-point.sh --approve --retain-until 2026-11-20
```
The knob's line was `datastore redis redis-server`. The probe before it (`--refresh-into --dry-run-into`) had raised no finding about it.

### Output
```
recovery-point: refused: datastore redis redis-server.service: its dump needs a login, to BGSAVE, and its aclfile sets the users, so its requirepass isn't one to try. Give its datastore line a user and key file (datastore redis <unit> <user> <key-file>), or cover it with a backup line
```

### What the Redis actually has
- **No `aclfile`.**
- `redis.conf` sets `requirepass`, then, nine lines later, an **inline `user default on …` line**, and `include`s a second file.
- `_probe-lib.sh` sets `RC_ACL=1` for either an `aclfile` or a `user` line (L714). Refusing to try `requirepass` there is defensible, since an inline `user default` can set a different password.
- The fix was the message's own advice: `datastore redis redis-server default /etc/credstore.encrypted/<cred>`. After that the dump, the chain's stop and the post-boot check all passed.

### Expected
1. **Text that names the actual cause.** For example: "its config sets the users (an `aclfile`, or a `user` line in `redis.conf`), so its `requirepass` isn't one to try." The four `aclfile sets the users` strings are at `_gate-lib.sh` L400 and L476 and `recovery-point.sh` L550, plus the usage text at L90. As written, an owner checks for an `aclfile`, finds none, and has reason to distrust the refusal.
2. **The probe raises it before the window.** A `datastore redis` line with no user, on a Redis where `RC_ACL` is 1, means `recovery-point.sh` will refuse. The reboot chain can't `SAVE` where its stop wouldn't persist either. The probe reads the same config (`RC_ACL`), so it could report a knob finding, such as `redis-login:<unit>`, naming the fix.
   - Here the refusal came at the recovery point, about 3 h before the window. On a host that takes its recovery point inside the window, it costs window time.

item.title: patching-hosts: a backup regime stops standing in for a dump after any boot, because systemd's reset state reads as "last run ended in success, so it isn't one to rely on"
item.body:
Found in host 6's second run of 2026-10-20 (process log `2026-09-28-host-6.md`; a private repo, so no identifiers here), at `468bf14`.

### Command
After an in-guest reboot (run 1's chain), a second run's recovery point:
```
bash skills/patching-hosts/scripts/recovery-point.sh --approve --retain-until 2026-11-20
```

### Output (`gate.backup_regime`)
```
{"unit":"<app>-backup.service","service":"<app>-backup.service","datastores":["postgresql@16-main.service"],
 "not_used":"<app>-backup.service's last run ended in success, so it isn't one to rely on"}
```
So it dumped Postgres itself. That gave the owner two files to copy off the node and attest instead of one. The same morning, before the boot, the same unit stood in for the dump.

Starting that run's bulk against run 1's recovery point instead was refused too:
```
backup unit <app>-backup.service hasn't started since the recovery point began: its last run started never
```
That refusal is right, but it shows the same blind spot: run 1's backup run happened, and the journal has it.

### Why
- **Where the regime is judged:** `recovery-point.sh` L364–369 decides from `systemctl show`, with `Result` success and a set `ExecMainExitTimestamp`.
- **What a boot does:** it resets both. A unit that hasn't run this boot reads `Result=success` (systemd's initial value) with an empty `ExecMainExitTimestamp`.
- **So:**
  - **The message contradicts itself.** "ended in success, so it isn't one to rely on" prints the default `Result` as if it were a run's outcome.
  - **Any boot since the regime's last run makes it unusable**, for a daily timer until its next tick. On a host that patches right after an earlier reboot, or one rebooted by the platform, the recovery point always falls back to dumps.

### Expected
1. **The last run read from the journal when systemd's state is empty.** The unit's own last invocation (`journalctl -u <svc> -o json`, its `_SYSTEMD_INVOCATION_ID` and the `UNIT_RESULT`/exit lines), or the timer's `LastTriggerUSec`, survive the boot where the journal is persistent. The recovery point starts the unit again anyway: the question is only whether it's a regime that has worked.
2. **The message says what it read:** "its last run isn't recorded since this boot (systemd's state resets at boot)", not "ended in success".

item.title: verify-facts.sh: a repo#N reference without an owner resolves against the current repo, giving TRUE about the wrong issue
item.body:
**What:** `verify-facts.sh --issues` reads a `repo#N` reference written without an owner as a bare `#N`. It then resolves it against the **current** repo (or `--repo`), and emits a confident TRUE row about the wrong issue.

The token grammar is `(\b[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)?#[0-9]+` ([verify-facts.sh:352](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/blob/main/skills/curating-context/scripts/verify-facts.sh#L352)). The optional group needs a slash, so `watcher#368` fails it and the bare `#368` matches.

**Measured 2026-10-20** against this repo at `ee6ccc1`:

```
$ bash skills/curating-context/scripts/verify-facts.sh --file skills/coordinating-epics/references/process-log.md --issues --repo gregoryfoster/skills
TRUE	issue	skills/coordinating-epics/references/process-log.md	#368	closed — check whether the prose still describes it as pending
```

The prose means **CannObserv/watcher#368**, which is OPEN ("[Epic] Headless Watcher and cohort boundaries"). The verdict is about **gregoryfoster/skills#368**, which is CLOSED and is a patching-hosts issue. The cohort writes this short form often. In this repo alone there are `skills#81` ×8, `skills#82` ×7, `watcher#368` ×5 and `processor#24` ×4 across SKILL.md and references. When the short name matches the current repo (`skills#81` here), the result is right only by coincidence.

**Why it matters:** a TRUE about the wrong issue is worse than UNVERIFIABLE. It tells the agent the reference was checked, and a "closed, check whether the prose still says pending" hint then sends it to rewrite prose about an issue it never cited.

**Proposal:** treat `<word>#N` (a bare match directly after `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]`) as its own shape:
- when `<word>` names the current repo, resolve it as today;
- otherwise emit UNVERIFIABLE with "short cross-repo reference `<word>#N`: no owner, so it can't be resolved; write `owner/<word>#N`". Guessing the owner from the current repo's org is tempting, but it's a guess, and FALSE/TRUE must stay command-backed.

**Already handled downstream:** #438's `stale-issue-prose.sh` declines to judge these rows (status `short-repo`), so the TypeSafe pass doesn't compound the error. The verifier's verdict is still wrong.

**Out of scope:** the TSV shape. A fix here changes only which verdict these rows get.

item.title: verify-facts.sh: a backticked path holding a tab splits its TSV row into six fields
item.body:
**What:** `verify-facts.sh` can emit a **six-column** TSV row. `check_paths` takes a backticked token as a path claim after excluding `[ <>*$|(){}]` ([verify-facts.sh:104](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/blob/main/skills/curating-context/scripts/verify-facts.sh#L104)). A tab isn't in that set, so a backticked path holding a literal tab is printed with the tab intact, and `emit()`'s `printf '%s\t…'` splits the claim across two fields.

**Measured 2026-10-20:**

```
$ printf 'see `src/a\tb.py` and #1\n' > TABDOC.md
$ bash skills/curating-context/scripts/verify-facts.sh --file TABDOC.md | awk -F'\t' '{print NF}'
6
```

**Why it matters:** the header promises `verdict<TAB>class<TAB>location<TAB>claim<TAB>evidence`. A consumer that holds rows to five columns refuses the whole file over one row, which is what #438's `stale-issue-prose.sh` did until CR 422 relaxed it to "issue rows only". Rare in practice; the contract is still broken.

**Proposal:** add `\t` to `check_paths`' exclusion set (`[[:space:]]` instead of the literal space would also cover a stray CR). As a backstop, `emit()` could replace tabs and newlines in its fields with a space, as `check_commands` already does for its claims ("keeps the emitted claim TSV-safe"). A structural test pinning "every row has five fields" over a fixture with a tab, a CR and a newline-adjacent token would hold it.

item.title: curating-context: stale-issue-prose.sh should skip archival docs by default (plans were its top false alarms)
item.body:
**What:** `stale-issue-prose.sh` (#438) judges every issue reference the verifier reports, including those in **archival** docs: dated plans, specs and process logs that the skill already treats as history (`ctx_is_archival` in `_context-lib.sh`, which Phase 1's measurement uses).

**Evidence from the #438 measurement** ([report](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/issues/438#issuecomment-6302036571)): the highest-scoring false alarms were plan documents. "Clear the eight open issues that accumulated from the #253/#254/#264 shipping cycle…" scored 0.66, and a plan's `done-when` table row scored 0.60. Each was true when written and describes a plan's scope, not the item's present state. At the default threshold (0.2), roughly two in three flags were false alarms.

**Proposal:** by default, mark occurrences in an archival path with a new status, `archival` (counted in the summary, not judged), so the agent's reading goes to live guidance first. Add `--include-archival` to judge them anyway. Use the skill's own matcher rather than a second notion of "archival". It is shell; the pass is Python. Call it the way `measure-context.sh` resolves it, or read the same `.skills/` knob, so the two can't disagree.

**Measure before changing the default:** re-run the #438 set with archival cases dropped and post the before/after sweep. The labelled set's sources and the evaluator command are on #438. Drop it if recall falls on the positives that live in plans. **Four of the 18 positives were in dated plan docs** (`docs/plans/`): two `still_open` and two of the three `already_done`. So a plain skip would cost a real share of the catch, and "archival" may need to mean something narrower than "under `docs/plans/`".

**Out of scope:** changing `verify-facts.sh`, which still reports these refs.

item.title: patching-hosts: a runtime from a third-party origin drifts silently, and there's no procedure for a pre-announced security release
item.body:
## Finding

A host's network-facing **language runtime came from a third-party apt origin** (a PHP PPA). The host's posture looked healthy:
- `unattended-upgrades` was enabled;
- the Ubuntu security count was low.

Even so, the runtime had sat **8 patch releases behind** for about eight months. `Allowed-Origins` never named the PPA, and no scheduled run ever took that origin.

This came to light when the PHP project **pre-announced** a critical security release: a fixed date and time, two CVSS 9.2 issues, with affected versions published only at release. The skill already has the pieces:
- the third-party class in the probe;
- `origin <origin> follow|pin|hold` in the knob;
- the expedited `apply.sh --lane origin:<origin>` the exe.dev profile prescribes for a Tailscale bulletin.

But nothing in the procedure says what to do with an advance notice. And `follow` puts a runtime's security fixes in the monthly maintenance lane by default.

## Asks

1. **Readings / policy: flag an origin that carries the serving runtime.**
   - When a third-party origin supplies a package that a listening or worker process maps, such as `php-fpm`, `node` or `python3` from a deadsnakes-style PPA, the probe should report that origin's pending set as a **security exposure**, not maintenance.
   - The knob gap list should name it when the origin has no expedite path.
   - A knob line such as `origin <origin> expedite` could mean: take it in the security lane, with approval, not only monthly.
2. **run.md: a "pre-announced release" procedure.**
   - **Before T:** record the before-versions (the rollback path), refresh the lists and confirm the origin is reachable. Take the recovery point now if the host has a data store, so it isn't taken under time pressure.
   - **After T:** poll `apt-cache policy <pkg>` until the fixed version appears. A PPA can lag the upstream tag by hours, so state the lag, never assume it. Then run the expedited lane with the owner's approval.
   - **Verify the runtime itself,** not just the package: `php -v` and `php-fpm -v`, a real request through the pool, and a reload (`-t` first) rather than a restart where the service supports one.
   - Record the CVE IDs when upstream publishes them.
3. **Environment profiles beyond exe.dev.** Two host shapes came up that the generic apt path covers only partly:
   - **A cloud VM with no local data store** (its database is a managed cluster). The recovery point is the package before-versions, and the reboot is the provider's power cycle.
   - **A local development VM under a desktop hypervisor.** Its data store is a dev database that still needs a dump. A "reboot" means the VM restarting from the host, and a host-mounted project tree affects what `needrestart` sees.
4. **"Outside apt" on the operator's workstation.** The same advance notice applies to a Homebrew-managed runtime, and a workstation tends to accumulate **end-of-life** runtime kegs that will never get the fix. A one-line note in readings.md would cover it: list installed runtime versions outside apt, and flag EOL ones as findings, not pending updates.

## Why it matters

The silent drift is the worse half. A host can pass every check the skill makes today and still serve traffic on a runtime months behind, because the origin that matters most was never followed at security cadence.

Filed from a consuming project's run (private; no identifiers here).

item.title: curating-context: CTX_ARCHIVAL doesn't reach measure-context.sh (Phase 1), and three prose copies of the archival list are unpinned
item.body:
Found by #463 ([report](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/issues/463#issuecomment-6321998680), "Proposed, not filed") and filed by the epic #451 coordinator. Not part of that epic.

**What:** curating-context's archival list (`plans specs research audits archive`) has one environment override and several unpinned copies:
- **`CTX_ARCHIVAL` moves only part of the skill.** `_context-lib.sh` reads it (`CTX_ARCHIVAL="${CTX_ARCHIVAL:-$CTX_ARCHIVAL_DEFAULT}"`), and so do `check-seams.sh`, `context-budget-guard.sh` and, since #463, `stale-issue-prose.sh`. But `measure-context.sh`, which runs Phase 1, keeps its own copy of the default and takes `--archival`, so it ignores `CTX_ARCHIVAL` [traced in #463: `measure-context.sh:208`, `:881`]. One setting can't move Phase 1 and the continuous surfaces together.
- **#463 pinned only the defaults:** the library's, `measure-context.sh`'s and the Python port's. Three **prose** copies of the list in help text are unpinned: `measure-context.sh:41`, `context-budget-guard.sh:52` and `context-delta.sh:37` [traced 2026-10-21: the two help-text copies spell it comma-separated, `(plans, specs, research, audits, archive)`, so a grep for the default string misses them].

**Why it matters:** a repo whose archive lives elsewhere (`docs/history/`) sets `CTX_ARCHIVAL=history`, and Phase 1 still counts those docs as live. The budget it measures and the docs the other surfaces skip then disagree, and nothing says so. The prose copies are where a reader learns the list, and they can drift silently.

**Suggested fix:**
1. `measure-context.sh` falls back to `CTX_ARCHIVAL` when `--archival` isn't given, so the flag wins, then the env var, then the default. Update its `--help` to say so.
2. Extend #463's parity test to the three prose copies, or generate them from the default.
3. Consider a `.skills/` knob only if a cohort repo actually needs a persistent override. Measure first: no repo has asked yet.

item.title: patching-hosts process log: 2026-10-21 cloud VM, dev VM, workstation (a pre-announced runtime release under advance approval; #464 executed)
item.body:
Process-log entry for gregoryfoster/skills, drafted from a consuming project's run (SKILL.md step 7), plus the promotion candidates it supports. It's the **execution record for the scenario #464 describes**: #464 was filed the morning of the release, before anything ran, and this entry is what happened when the procedure met a real release. **The consuming repo is private, so the entry names no identifier of its own:** hosts are described by shape. No security update from this release is pending on any of the three hosts.

**The operator expects this to recur** (every PHP, Node or Python security release reaches a third-party origin this way), so the candidates below aim to make it a scripted path, not a hand run.

**To land:**
- Add the entry below as `references/process-log/2026/2026-10-21-three-hosts-pre-announced-release.md`. (Three hosts in one run don't fit `<date>-<host>.md`, so name it as you prefer.)
- Add this row to `references/process-log/2026/index.md`:

```
| [2026-10-21](2026-10-21-three-hosts-pre-announced-release.md) | cloud VM, dev VM, workstation | Hand run (scripts not wired in) of a pre-announced PHP release under advance owner approval. Upstream shipped 23 min early; the PPA's installable binaries lagged 4 h 40 m (amd64) and 6 h (arm64). Release-day CDN 503s failed the first apply at fetch, so download-first, then --no-download. The web server's /health never reached the runtime |
```

## Promotion candidates

Numbered against #464's asks where they refine one.

1. **run.md, the pre-announced-release procedure (#464 ask 2): watch the install channel, per architecture, and state the lags measured below.** The upstream tag is not an install signal. The PPA's own `Packages` index for each architecture is, and Launchpad's build API gives a readable intermediate state ("built, not yet published"). A watcher must keep **per-channel failure streaks**: one healthy channel must not mask another's errors (lesson 3).
2. **apply.sh / run.md §3: make the set all-or-nothing against the origin's CDN.** Prefetch every candidate `.deb` with retries (`apt-get install -d -o Acquire::Retries=N`, looped), gate on all of them being in the cache, then install with `--no-download`. `probe.sh --dry-run-into` already downloads the set into `DIR/archives`; the apply could consume that cache and refuse when it's incomplete (lesson 2).
3. **readings.md: a list refresh can exit 0 and still be stale.** `apt-get update` exited 0 with `Err:`/`Ign:` lines on the origin's `Packages`, and the stale candidate looked exactly like "not released yet". The probe should read each origin's fetch result from the update's own output, and report a stale list as `unknown`, not as current (lesson 2).
4. **The generic-apt self-restart table (#464 ask 2's "reload rather than restart"):** `php<ver>-fpm`'s maintainer script **restarts** the service on upgrade, whatever the operator would choose; a reload only happens if `policy-rc.d` blocks it. Measured under 1 s with an `ondemand` pool. Record it with the other self-restarting packages, and drop "reload where supported" for this package unless the skill blocks the maintainer restart on purpose (lesson 4).
5. **run.md, verification (#464 ask 2's "verify the runtime itself"):** a health endpoint the **web server answers on its own** proves nothing about the runtime behind it. Verify with requests that pass through the pool, compared against a **baseline taken through the same path before the apply**: status, size, and for an API response, the bytes. Expect a cold opcode cache: the first request ran 1.75× the baseline and was back at baseline by the third (lesson 5).
6. **run.md §2, the recovery point under a pre-announced release (#464 ask 2):** taking it **before T** is right, but it goes stale while the channel lags. Take a second one **right before the apply** as well. The pair is also evidence: diffing them explained a post-apply change the run would otherwise have pinned on the runtime (lesson 6).
7. **The iron law and advance approval.** The owner gave one approval in the session, before T, covering a named package set, three named hosts, the checks per host, and "a failed check stops the run before the next host"; the apply then ran as each channel landed, hours later. The skill should say whether a **scoped, conditional, in-session approval given in advance** satisfies "approval given in the host's own session" for a pre-announced release. This run treated it as satisfying the law, and the scope held (lesson 7).
8. **A remote-driven apply runs as a transient unit.** Where the operator's session reaches the host over SSH rather than running on it, wrap the apply in `systemd-run --unit=<name> --wait --pipe --collect`, so a dropped connection can't leave dpkg half-configured. (The skill's own reboot chain already uses `systemd-run`.)
9. **readings.md, "outside apt" on the workstation (#464 ask 4):** the Homebrew checklist in lesson 8. Most of all: **upgrading an unversioned formula re-links it over a force-linked, keg-only versioned one,** so the runtime on PATH silently changes minor line. Verify `<runtime> -v` after every workstation upgrade.
10. **A `-t` config test is a root check.** `php-fpm<ver> -t` run without root fails with "FPM initialization failed" on a valid config. Run every config test as root, or it reads as a finding that isn't one.

---

## Session 2026-10-21 — cloud VM, dev VM, workstation

A **hand run of the skill's procedure**: the scripts are vendored but not wired into this consumer, so each step was run by hand, following SKILL.md and run.md. The trigger was the PHP project's **pre-announced critical release** (two CVSS 9.2 issues, announced the day before for 14:00 UTC). Three hosts were in scope:
- **a cloud VM** with no local data store (its database is a managed cluster), on Ubuntu 24.04, PHP from the `ondrej/php` PPA, amd64;
- **a dev VM** under a desktop hypervisor, with a local MariaDB dev database and a host-mounted project tree, the same PPA, arm64;
- **the operator's workstation**, PHP from Homebrew.

A fourth host was **recorded out of scope by the owner**, with the reason recorded in the consumer.

### Decisions

- **Owner approval, given once before T** (candidate 7): auto-apply on all three hosts as each one's fixed build appears, with the checks per host named, and any failed check stopping the run before the next host.
- **The workstation's EOL runtime kegs were retired** before the release, with the owner's approval. The release then confirmed it: the oldest supported line got no release.
- **Scope was the runtime's packages alone.** Every other pending package stayed held, for the hosts' own scheduled runs.

### Readings and prep (before T)

- **Before-versions recorded** on each host. The cloud VM was **8 patch releases behind**: #464's finding.
- **Lists refreshed, and the origin confirmed reachable**, on both apt hosts.
- **Recovery point on the dev VM:** `mysqldump --single-transaction --routines --triggers --events`, written through the host mount, which takes it off the VM; each dump checked for its `-- Dump completed` trailer, and its sha256 recorded. It went in a **subdirectory**, because a sibling tool picks "the newest `*.sql.gz`" from the parent directory and would have loaded a dev dump as a production one. The cloud VM has no data store, so its rollback is the before-versions.
- **Baselines taken through the runtime:** a front page and an API namespace index, through the local vhost on each host. Plus the dev VM's full unit test tier, which passed.
- **CI** (a hosted runner with a setup action) resolves the latest patch release by itself; its baseline was read from the last run's log.

### Timeline of the release, UTC (candidate 1)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| ~13:37 | **Upstream released, 23 min before the announced time.** Fixed: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. The changelog named both advisories at release (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w, GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp, both in Core). |
| 14:13–14:31 | Homebrew bump PRs opened. |
| 14:36 | PPA builds dispatched, all architectures. |
| 14:45 | PPA source publication accepted. |
| 15:57 | PPA **amd64 built**. |
| 16:38 | Homebrew versioned-formula PR merged. |
| ~17:00 | Its bottle for the workstation's tag visible in the formula API, about 20 min after the merge. **Workstation, minor line patched.** |
| 17:46 | PPA **arm64 built**. |
| ~18:10 | Homebrew unversioned formula's bottle visible. **Workstation done.** |
| ~18:16 | PPA **amd64 published**, 2 h 19 m after it was built. |
| 18:25 | **Cloud VM done**, after one failed attempt (lesson 2). |
| ~19:36 | PPA **arm64 published**, 1 h 50 m after it was built. |
| 19:47 | **Dev VM done.** |

From the upstream tag to an installable package: **about 4 h 40 m (amd64) and 6 h (arm64)**. Most of the lag was between "built" and "published". At 16:52, Launchpad's binary-publication API had **no record at all** of the amd64 build finished an hour earlier, not even a pending one.

### Lessons

#### 1. The watched channel must be the install channel

A watcher polled five channels every 5 minutes: the upstream release JSON, the PPA's `Packages.gz` for each architecture, and the Homebrew formula API (filtered on a bottle for the host's own tag, read from `brew ruby -e 'puts Utils::Bottles.tag'`). It exited on the first channel to change. Then that host was patched and the watcher re-armed for the rest. The upstream channel fired first and was useful only as information. Each install channel arrived on its own clock, hours apart.

#### 2. Release-day CDN 503s, and the all-or-nothing set (candidates 2, 3)

The PPA's CDN served **intermittent HTTP 503s for hours**: on the indexes, then on the `.deb`s.
- `apt-get update` **exited 0** after `Err:`/`Ign:` lines on the origin's `Packages`. The stale candidate was indistinguishable from "not released yet".
- **The cloud VM's first apply failed at fetch:** 5 of 11 `.deb`s returned 503, apt exited 100 after 4 minutes, and it never reached dpkg. Nothing was installed: `dpkg --audit` clean, the old version still running, the service untouched. The 6 that downloaded stayed in apt's cache.
- **The second pass split download from install:** a loop of `apt-get install -y -d -o Acquire::Retries=5 --only-upgrade '<pattern>'`, with a 30 s pause, up to 30 attempts, gated on every candidate being in the cache. Then `apt-get install --no-download -o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold` under `NEEDRESTART_MODE=l`. The cloud VM got its set on attempt 1 of the loop, the dev VM on attempt 2.

That split is what turns the 503s from a gamble into a non-event: dpkg sees the whole set or nothing.

#### 3. A watcher that masks one channel's failures with another's success (candidate 1)

The first watcher counted a poll as healthy when **any** channel fetched. With the PPA's indexes on 503 and Homebrew's API answering, it stayed silent about the PPA for about an hour. That would have meant a late patch, not a wrong one. Fixed with a failure streak per channel, three retries per poll, and an error after six failed polls in a row.

#### 4. The FPM package restarts itself (candidate 4)

On both apt hosts, `php8.4-fpm`'s maintainer script **restarted** the service (a new main PID) during configure. Measured: under 1 s, `pm = ondemand`. `needrestart` in list mode listed nothing for the runtime. On the dev VM it listed `dbus`, `systemd-logind`, `unattended-upgrades` and the user manager, all from the VM's own unrelated backlog, since PHP maps none of their libraries. The FPM drop-ins in `conf.d/` and `pool.d/` survived, confirmed by `php-fpm -tt`. No `.dpkg-dist` or `.dpkg-new` files appeared.

#### 5. A health check that never reaches the runtime (candidate 5)

The site's `/health` is answered by **the web server itself**, with a static 200, so it was green throughout and proved nothing about PHP. The checks that counted went through the pool: the front page (status and size) and an API index (byte-identical …

item.title: patching-hosts process log: 2026-10-21 co-status (first run; the dry run counts 0 against stale host lists)
item.body:
Process-log entry for `patching-hosts`, drafted in the consuming repo (CannObserv/status#54) per *Adding an entry*: the skill is vendored there, so the entry lands here. The host repo is public; all security updates in it are applied. Index row and entry file below.

### Index row (`process-log/2026/index.md`)

```
| [2026-10-21](2026-10-21-co-status.md) | co-status | First run of a new host under the scripts. 90 in the maintenance lane, 507 s (2.9× dry run); 11 s down. The dry run counted 0 against the host's 28-day-old lists, so the bulk refused until a host `apt-get update`. Node Tailscale auto-update on under a tailnet default of off |
```

### Entry file (`process-log/2026/2026-10-21-co-status.md`)

## Session 2026-10-21 — co-status (first run under the scripts)

Host repo: CannObserv/status (public); tracking issue CannObserv/status#54.

### Environment

- `exe-dev-exeuntu`, generation `newer`; guestd layout; journal persistent; `/tmp` under the `d` rule (kept at boot). Platform kernel 6.12.93 before the boot, 6.12.113 after: the platform moved it, not the run.
- One local Postgres 16 cluster (`status`, `status_dev`, `status_test`), two uvicorn services, three oneshot timers (two sweeps every 60 s, an hourly drift check). No Redis, no Qdrant, Docker and nginx disabled.
- No knob before this run: the first probe was report-only against `automatic`.

### Readings

- First probe, no knob: 62 security (lower bound), 26 `-updates`, Tailscale 1 pending; apt timers masked and `Periodic::Enable "0"` from `docker-disable-periodic-update` (image); needrestart drop-in already present; Tailscale `AutoUpdate.Apply` true on the node although the owner had turned it off tailnet-wide.
- Knob written: `posture scheduled`, one window, an `inflight` over the sweep and drift units, two `service` lines, two `health` lines, `datastore postgres postgresql@16-main status status_dev`, `exception database:status_test`, `origin Tailscale pin <version>`.
- Maintenance-lane dry run: 88 packages, 176 s, 264 MiB, 98 MiB download, no conffile prompts, no removals. No hold group pending.
- Bulk: 90 upgraded, exit 0, 507 s (2.9× the dry run), 260 MiB; health 2/2 on the first poll. The two extra packages arrived with the bulk's own list refresh, 30 minutes after the dry run.
- Reboot decision: needrestart listed dbus, logind, journald, timesyncd, polkit, cron, packagekit, Postgres, both app services, the systemd manager and the user manager; PID 1 mapped 15 deleted files; no `reboot-required`.
- Chain: clean. API down 11 s (stop 19:11:18Z, active 19:11:29Z), Postgres back at the same second. `--post-boot`: every check green; the only finding `setup-script:present`.

### What the skill got wrong or lacked

1. **The dry run counts against the host's own lists, which masked timers leave stale.** The first `probe.sh --lane maintenance --dry-run-into` counted **0** (and flagged `lists:stale`, 672 h): `unattended-upgrade --dry-run` reads `/var/lib/apt/lists`, not the `--refresh-into` copy, and the host's lists were 28 days old. A 0 count makes the bulk refuse ("counted nothing"), so the run needs a host `apt-get update` before the dry run, which `run.md` §3 only places inside the bulk. Proposed: the dry run refreshes the host's lists first (it already runs as root and downloads the set), or refuses with that instruction when `lists:stale` is raised, rather than writing a 0-count summary.
2. **Tailscale auto-update: the tailnet default was off and the node's own pref was on.** The owner had disabled auto-update tailnet-wide, but `tailscale debug prefs` read `Apply: true`: an explicit node setting outlives a tailnet default. The profile covers the reverse (the tailnet default re-applied over a node's off). Both directions need the node set too; after `tailscale set --auto-update=false` it held through the reboot.
3. **The setup-script containment's first half has to precede the boot.** With the file absent between boots, `setup-script:redelivered` gives the remedy "once it's back on disk"; the order that worked was CannObserv/provisioner#4's: `systemctl disable` before the reboot, `chmod 600` after it. The re-delivered file ran 0 times this boot and came back at 0755; `--post-boot` names the key-shaped line, which is the useful prompt to revoke. The owner revoked the key (a Tailscale auth key) the same day, and the knob now declares `exception setup-script:redelivered`.

### Decisions

- Posture `scheduled` (monthly), both lanes in one window; Tailscale `pin`, not `follow`.
- `status_test` excepted rather than dumped: the suite rebuilds it.
- The deploy of the repo's own dependency bumps (five Dependabot PRs) ran after the post-boot checks, in the same window, so the reboot and the deploy restarts weren't stacked.

### Surprises

- `/tmp` held 115 leftovers from the host repo's own test suite (a test that fails every `rm -rf` also fails the deploy script's EXIT-trap cleanup): `environment.tmp.staged` was the only reading that surfaced it. CannObserv/status#53.
- The dump-copy hint (`ssh <host> 'sudo cat …' > file`) worked as written; the owner's copies matched on the first try.

item.title: curating-context: verify-facts.sh's command scan still toggles fences naively; port the CommonMark rule
item.body:
**What:** `verify-facts.sh`'s `check_commands` decides which text is code with a naive fence toggle ([`verify-facts.sh:178`](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/blob/64626e8a/skills/curating-context/scripts/verify-facts.sh#L178)):

```awk
/^[[:space:]]*```/ { fence = !fence; next }
```

Any line that starts with three backticks flips the state:

- Inside a ```` fence, a quoted ``` line "closes" it.
- A `~~~` fence is never seen.
- A prose line starting "\`\`\`json\`\`\` blocks" opens a fence that runs to the next ```.

From that point to the end of the file, prose is scanned as code and code as prose.

**Why it matters:** this is now the last fence rule in curating-context that disagrees with CommonMark. #441 (`972a469e`) moved the three gate walks (`check-counts.sh`, `check-seams.sh`, `prove-no-loss.sh`) to one shared `fence_toggle`. `_sentences.py` and `measure-context.sh` already followed CommonMark. Out of sync, `check_commands` reads English as commands (the false matches its own comment warns about) and misses commands inside the fences it lost track of. Raised in #441's review as CR 466 and held, because #441's brief put `verify-facts.sh` out of scope.

**Proposal:** port `measure-context.sh`'s awk fence rule ([`measure-context.sh:1321–1346`](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/blob/64626e8a/skills/curating-context/scripts/measure-context.sh#L1321-L1346)) into `check_commands`:

- A run of 3 or more backticks or tildes opens a fence, unless the info string of a backtick opener holds a backtick.
- A fence closes only on a run of its own character at least as long as the opener, with nothing after it.
- A trailing CR is stripped first.

**Decide while porting:** which indentation rule applies. `measure-context.sh` takes `indent < 4`, which is CommonMark's. The three gate walks (`fence_toggle`) and `_sentences._FENCE` take any indentation, because a fence inside a list item is indented past three spaces. Pick one for `verify-facts.sh` and say why. Ideally the two families agree, or the difference is named.

**Test:** a `test_fence_close.py` case for `check_commands`. A command in prose after a ```` block quoting one ```bash line must not be extracted, and one inside the block must be. Confirm it fails under the current toggle.

**Related:** #461, #462 (`verify-facts.sh`), #275, #441.

item.title: tightened-rules: count a rule delegated behind a link as kept — measured on #442's set before anything changes
item.body:
Follow-up to #442, filed by the epic #451 coordinator. **Decided 2026-10-23 by the operator:** keep `tightened-rules.sh`'s default threshold at 0.3, and **measure** whether a rule delegated behind a link should count as kept **before** changing anything. This issue is that measurement, plus the change if the numbers support it.

**What:** `tightened-rules.sh` (#442) sees only a tightened sentence's **successor section**. When a curation moves a rule into a reference doc and leaves a link, the pass reads it as dropped. That's the class-B *demote* the rubric prescribes. On #442's random slice that is **18 of 26 positives** ("survive only as a link to another doc or in another section") [[#442 report](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/issues/442#issuecomment-6357235012)]. The doc tells the agent to look elsewhere before restoring. These flags are cheap to clear by hand, but they're half of what a run flags at 0.3 (79 of 150 on R).

**Proposal, in order. Stop at the first step that answers it:**
1. **Code only.** For each sentence the pass would send, follow the links in its successor section to the destination doc (at the same tree, as `prove-no-loss.sh` resolves `--docs-dir` / `--also`). If the sentence is `kept` there (the same substring test as today, measured harmless in CR 469), status `delegated`, and nothing is sent. This costs nothing per run. Measure how many of the set's delegated positives it resolves, and that it resolves no true drop.
2. **Only if step 1 leaves a real share unresolved:** a second Noul, "Does `linked_section` state what `sentence` requires or forbids?", with the linked destination section as state. Asked only where the successor links somewhere, so it's one extra call on those sentences.
3. **Decide the default from the numbers.** If `delegated` removes false re-reads and costs no true drop, it becomes default-on with an opt-out flag. Otherwise it stays opt-in, or the issue closes as not planned, with the numbers. Either is a fine outcome for the epic.

**Measuring it:**
- **#442's committed set is the base:** `tests/fixtures/typesafe-eval/tightened-rules/`, 421 sentences from 49 curations in 9 public repos.
- **Labels:** the current label says *yes* for "moved behind a link", because the pass saw only the successor. This child needs a **second label column** on the delegated positives: *held at the destination*, or *not*. Add it beside `labels.tsv`, appending, never re-sampling (#441's lesson).
- **Inputs:** `inputs.jsonl` holds each record's successor but not the link targets' text. Recover the destinations from the same public clones at each curation commit, and re-check visibility at commit time (the fixture README, step 1).
- **Report** the R-slice flag count and catches at 0.3, with and without `delegated`, plus every true drop it would have hidden. **The pass exists for recall:** hiding one real drop costs more than a hundred cleared re-reads.

**Hazards:**
- **A link is a claim, not proof.** A pointer to a doc that doesn't hold the rule is exactly the drop the iron law guards. The substring test is the floor; a looser match needs its own measurement.
- **`prove-no-loss.sh` stays byte-unchanged.** If the pass needs destination paths, extend `--candidates`' records (output only), and prove the identity again on the 66 real curations, as #442 did.
- **Docs:** `references/keep-cut-rubric.md`'s tightened-rules subsection (SKILL.md byte-unchanged).

**Out of scope:** the 0.3 threshold (decided), and subtle weakenings ("must" becoming "is"), which #442 documented as a limit.

item.title: tightened-rules: ask `dropped` once per successor section, one question per sentence — measured on #442's set before it changes
item.body:
Found while working #470 ([corrections, item 8](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/issues/470#issuecomment-6366374087)). It's out of #470's scope because it changes the request #442 measured.

**What:** `tightened-rules.sh` sends one request per sentence. Its state is `{sentence, heading?, after_section}`, and the successor section is most of every request. The sentences that share a successor resend it once each. TypeSafe's batching is several questions over **one** state, billed once (the docs' *Parallel questions* cookbook: 13 questions in one call cost 12.2× less than 13 calls). There is no multi-state request.

**Measured on #442's pool** (1,102 records from 66 curations, the shipped code):
- 854 sendable sentences share **214** successors: median 2 per successor, mean 4, max 82.
- One request per successor, one `dropped` question per sentence (naming `sentences[i]`), cuts requests about **4×**. By the client's byte estimate it cuts input about **2.9×**. The instructions are still sent once per question, which is why the cut is under 4×.

**What it buys, honestly sized:** at today's price the set's 421 requests are about 529k input tokens, roughly $0.02, and took about 41 s sequentially (#442's eval). A curation sends a median of 7.5 sentences and at most 82. So this is latency and rate-limit headroom at the 82-sentence tail, not money. **Low priority.**

**To do it:**
1. Restate `DROPPED` against `sentences[i]` and `after_section`. Re-measure on the committed 421-case set (`typesafe-eval.py`, a new cache), in the batched shape it would ship in. Keep it only if Brier and the 0.3 row hold (#442: 0.139, 52 · 128 · 9 · 232). A question that can see sibling sentences may answer differently, and that's the risk to measure.
2. Chunk a successor's sentences under the client's guards: 32k tokens per question (state plus one question) and 64k per request.
3. `--dry-run`'s case format and the set's per-sentence `expected` must still score per sentence. The evaluator keys metrics by question name, so this needs a design: one case per request with N named questions, or a name per ordinal.

**Siblings:** `stale-issue-prose.sh` and `bare-digit-counts.sh` also ask one request per item, but their state is small: a sentence plus issue metadata, or a clause. Batching there saves round trips, not tokens. Check them only if latency becomes a complaint.

**Out of scope:** the wording itself, and the 0.3 threshold (decided on #470).

item.title: coordinating-epics: process-log entry - 2026-10-23 broker (CannObserv/broker#22)
item.body:
A process-log entry for `coordinating-epics`, from a run on a host that vendors this repo as a submodule. Per *Adding an entry*, it comes here as an issue: writing it into the vendored copy would leave the host with a modified submodule. The host repo, CannObserv/broker, is public, so the entry names it.

**Please add** the entry below as `process-log/2026/2026-10-23-broker.md`, and its row to `process-log/2026/index.md`.

**For #404:**
- **Finding 7 is a second sighting of #413** (`replace-section` can't rename a heading). No new issue.
- **Finding 8 is a new tool gap,** not yet filed: `scan.sh` reads every cross-repo ref with the host's token.
- **Promotion candidates** (each now seen in two runs): finding 5 with CannObserv/broker#80's 2026-10-14 finding 123 (a doc at its budget is a shared surface), and finding 6 with #428's finding 1 (foreign ticks).

---

## Session 2026-10-23 — CannObserv/broker#22

A design-doc epic: broker's production units moved from the dev checkout to root-owned releases under `/srv/broker`, built by a new `scripts/deploy.sh`. The way in was an approved design (D1-D11) whose Steps table became seven native sub-issues, CannObserv/broker#105 to CannObserv/broker#111. It closed on 2026-10-23 on its exit criterion, after an empty re-scan. The parent epic, CannObserv/broker#80 (logged 2026-10-14), was burning down the same repo's backlog on the same host at the same time, coordinated from its own thread.

### Shape
- **Way in:** a design doc's Steps table, with one tiebreak set from the parent (a released upstream dependency pre-empts the next child, between children).
- **Children:** 7 planned, 7 closed. Mid-run issues: 13 (CannObserv/broker#112 to CannObserv/broker#124), all out of epic (the parent's backlog, a sibling epic's, or follow-ups filed at the end).
- **Check-ins:** creation, 7 check-ins, plus three between-check-in entries (a cross-repo request filed with approval, a floating child started beside a parent child, and a monitor going ready).
- **Days:** 2026-10-17 to 2026-10-23.
- **Stats:** the node's sourced baseline went from 467/4 (`tests/deploy`) and 837/4 (full suite) to 722/4 and 1261/4, with the same four skips throughout. `ACL LOG` stayed at 4 entries from the first read to the last.

### What was different
- **Every child changed production,** one unit at a time; three children ran a rollback drill. Verification read journals, `_UID`s, state files and the deploy log, not merges.
- **Two coordinators shared one deploy script.** The parent's children deployed through the script this epic was building, from C3 on.
- **The coordinator's pre-flight changed a child's scope twice:** C5's `backup.env` edit, and C7's budget question. Both went to the operator as recommendations in the child's thread, before any build.

### Findings that changed the protocol
1. **Two epics deploying through one script need a written rule, not a lock.** `deploy.sh` held a `flock`, which serializes two deploys but doesn't stop the second from rolling the first back: it accepts any CI-green ancestor of `origin/main`. Both coordinators' briefs carried the same rule: before each deploy, read the live symlink and the deploy journal, and deploy only `origin/main`'s tip. Whoever deploys second ships both. That held with no incident while a floating child and a parent child built and deployed side by side, and through the parent's later deploys. **A drill breaks the rule on purpose,** so the rule needs a named exception: the operator approved "back to `<sha>`" by sha in the child's thread.
2. **For a child that changes a unit and its environment together, brief both directions of the switch.** The scope for C5 (drop root) said to edit a host env file that every installed version of the unit reads. Edited before the deploy, the switch back would restore the old unit against the edited file, and both would fail (exit 4, nothing answering). Edited after, the new unit's forced run couldn't read the old path, and the deploy would switch back. The brief's recommendation: put both values in the unit and leave the host file alone. The implementer found a third reader, the restore runbook, which made the case stronger. The rule: for each host file a changed unit reads, ask what the old unit sees after a switch back, and what the new unit sees during its first forced run.
3. **Read drill journals for what ran, not only whether it passed.** One drill tick reported the new build under the old unit. The cause: a timer that fired in the ~0.25 s between the symlink swap and `daemon-reload`. Harmless for that child, but it mattered for the one where code and unit changed together, so it was carried there, and in the end written down as an accepted limit.
4. **Rehearse undocumented runtime behaviour with the unit file itself, before the merge, uploading nothing.** Whether `LoadCredential=` reads its source before `TemporaryFileSystem=` hides it wasn't in systemd 255's man pages. The brief proposed a `systemd-run -p` rehearsal. The implementer corrected that: properties sent over D-Bus may not expand `%d` the way a parsed unit file does. So the real unit file, rewritten by `sed`, ran as a runtime unit in `/run/systemd/system/`, then a second unit with the previous shape proved the rollback's ownership flip. That settled a question a previous child had left open. The brief rule: name the rehearsal's vehicle, and prefer the shipped artifact over a reconstruction of it.
5. **A doc at its budget is a shared surface (second run).** At the last child's hand-off, the policy file had 8 tokens of headroom, and the recovery runbook was 1.4k tokens over its budget. Each of the two previous children had noted the overage and left it for "the rewrite". The pre-flight measured both exactly from the repo's context metrics, and turned the Verify item "budgets hold" into an operator question before the build. The answer was to move dated history to an archive doc. **Rule:** at each hand-off, read the exact headroom of every doc the child will touch, and when a child defers an overage, name the child that will pay it.
6. **With native sub-issues, GitHub ticked the epic's box when a child closed, whoever closed it.** Seen on C4, C5 and C7 at least. Each tick was verified first, then accepted with `--accept-ticks`. The parent run found auto-ticks unreliable with plain task lists; with sub-issues they were consistent. That was still a claim each time, never evidence.
7. **`replace-section` can't rename a heading.** Retiring the design brief's "Interim" convention needed a new heading. The section kept its old heading, with a "Retired" line leading its new body. Second sighting of #413.
8. **`scan.sh` reads every cross-repo ref with the host repo's token.** One ref in a repo that token can't see returned a 404 warning at every check-in, and the coordinator had to read it by hand with that repo's own token. A per-owner token map, or a `--token-env OWNER=VAR` flag, would close the gap.
9. **Hand a parent epic its changes as a ready-to-write comment.** The last child rewrote the parent's verify recipe, which this coordinator doesn't own. The implementer posted the replacement text, part by part, on the child. The closing report on the parent links it, for the parent's coordinator to write through `epic-edit.sh`. The same was done for this epic's own retired section. Neither coordinator edited the other's body.
10. **An approval given in the operator's session was posted on the issue, quoted and timestamped,** by the implementing thread ("Operator approval, given in the agent session at ..."). Each scope change and each sudo step then had an auditable approval on the child, which the coordinator could cite at verification. Worth adding to the implementer contract.

### What the scripts caught
- `epic-edit.sh`'s lint refused a short cross-repo ref (`status#51`) in a note.
- `--dry-run`'s diff showed that a `note` re-stated a field already on the line (`note` appends), before the write.
- `--scan` refused nothing this run: every new issue was in the log line before the write.

| [2026-10-23](2026-10-23-broker.md) | CannObserv/broker#22 | Design-doc epic, 7 children moving production onto releases, beside its parent epic on one host. A tip-only deploy rule across two coordinators; brief both directions of a unit's switch; rehearse with the unit file itself; a doc at budget is a shared surface (2nd run) |

epic.goal: Turns the thirteen TypeSafe proposals (#435–#447) into opt-in, advisory steps in the skills they name. Each step calls TypeSafe's Jev model for a narrow typed judgment, and none changes a verdict, a gate or a GitHub write. - No network in the pytest suite. Structural tests use a fake transport, and live calls run only under `-m integration` (billed, never gated). Proposed at creation.
- A labelled set drawn from a private cohort repo is never committed to this public repo. Only its aggregate result is posted. Proposed at creation.

A reference may carry its own script-resolution block, held by `test_per_script_resolution.py`'s `REFERENCE_BLOCKS`: decided 2026-10-20 (#438 C1).
- The model is pinned to `jev-1.13.0` across the epic. Moving to a later version is its own child, re-measured. Proposed at creation.
- A proposal whose measurement shows no useful agreement is closed as not planned, with the numbers. That is a successful outcome for this epic, not a failure. Proposed at creation.

item.body:
Process-log entry for `patching-hosts`, drafted in the consuming repo (CannObserv/status#56) per *Adding an entry*. The skill is vendored there, so the entry lands here. The host repo is public. **Two packages are still pending on the host, one of them from `-security`**, and neither is named below. Per the third rule, land this after the host's next monthly window (Wed 17:00–23:00 UTC) has applied them. CannObserv/status will say so on this issue.

### Index row (`process-log/2026/index.md`)

```
| [2026-10-23](2026-10-23-co-status.md) | co-status | A bulletin's out-of-cycle window on a pinned origin (TS-2026-013): the lane takes only a follow origin, so the pin moved by hand and Tailscale went in by hand, outside apply.sh's gate and record. ~2.2 s tailnet gap, timed between 60 s sweeps that reach the API over the tailnet. needrestart's post-step list named the app services for a platform remediation's `uv self update` the day before |
```

### Entry file (`process-log/2026/2026-10-23-co-status.md`)

## Session 2026-10-23 — co-status (a bulletin on a pinned origin)

Host repo: CannObserv/status (public); tracking issue CannObserv/status#56; cohort coordination CannObserv/provisioner#77 (Tailscale TS-2026-013).

### Environment

- `exe-dev-exeuntu`, the same host as 2026-10-21's entry. The knob is `posture scheduled`, `datastore postgres …`, and `origin Tailscale pin 1.102.4`.
- Two uvicorn services bound to the tailnet address, launched with `uv run`. Two oneshot sweeps run every 60 s, and each pass GETs the production API's `/ready` **over the tailnet name**. An hourly drift check also runs.

### Readings

- Before: `tailscale version --daemon` 1.102.4 (go1.26.6), client and daemon. `apt-cache policy tailscale` candidate 1.104.2 from `pkgs.tailscale.com`. No apt pin for `tailscale` under `/etc/apt/preferences.d/`. `apt-mark showhold` empty, `dpkg --audit` clean, no `reboot-required`.
- Simulation: `apt-get -s install --only-upgrade tailscale=1.104.2` took `tailscale` alone.
- Run: `NEEDRESTART_MODE=l apt-get install --only-upgrade tailscale=1.104.2 </dev/null`, pinned, without `-y`, rc 0, 9.5 s.
- `tailscaled`: `got signal terminated` 14:01:24.468Z, `Starting -> Running` 14:01:26.704Z, so the gap was **~2.2 s**. That matches co-provisioner's 2.0 s and 2.2 s and co-processor's 2.3 s.
- After: client and daemon 1.104.2, go1.27.3. The new `MainPID`'s `ActiveEnterTimestamp` was the restart's proof.
- Health 2/2. API PIDs unchanged. The first sweep pass after the gap was green end to end: notifier, the API's `/ready` over the tailnet, and three healthchecks.io pings.

### What the skill got wrong or lacked

1. **A pinned origin has no lane for a bulletin.** `policy.md` routes a bulletin to `apply.sh --lane origin:<origin>`, and that lane takes a *follow* origin only: "The lane never takes a pinned or held one: a pin moves only by hand." So moving the knob's pin to the fix's version still leaves no scripted way to install it. The run went outside `apply.sh` entirely: no gate, no before-versions record, no `<run>` directory, no reprobe, and the recovery point's rule had to be judged by hand (no data-store package was in the set, so none was taken). Proposed: `--lane origin:<origin>` accepts a `pin` origin and installs exactly the pinned version (`<pkg>=<version>`), refusing when the candidate differs. Moving the pin stays a hand edit to the knob, and the install gets the lane's gate and record.
2. **`inflight` reads only what's running now, not what starts inside the step.** The knob's `inflight` was 0. But a 60 s sweep that starts during tailscaled's ~2 s restart would fail its `/ready` check over the tailnet and send a `/fail` ping, a false page. The run was timed by hand to start 20–30 s into the minute, with the sweeps firing at :06–:11. `run.md` already gates on `apt-daily-upgrade.timer`'s span (calendar plus random delay). Proposed: the same span check for each timer whose unit the knob's `inflight` names, against a step's expected duration (for one origin's restart, seconds).
3. **needrestart's list after a step names services the step didn't touch.** After a `tailscale`-only step, `needrestart -m u -b -r l` listed both app services. The cause was a day older: their `uv run` launcher maps a deleted `/usr/local/bin/uv`, replaced by `sudo uv self update` at 2026-10-22T18:16:48Z. That ran in the sequence that ends `exeuntu update claude/codex/…` and installs `libnss3-tools`, consistent with exe.dev's `remediate-emudhra-compromise` (claim; the journal shows the commands, not their caller). Read alone, the list blames the step and asks for restarts the step didn't cause. Proposed: take needrestart's list before each step and report the step's own additions apart from what was already there. Profile fact: on exeuntu, a `uv run`-launched service shows up as an obsolete binary after any `uv self update` (measured 2026-10-23, co-status).

### Decisions

- A hand run, pinned by version, under `NEEDRESTART_MODE=l`, owner-approved in the host's session. The knob's pin moved to `1.104.2` in the same change.
- No recovery point: the set was `tailscale` alone, and no data-store package or library was mapped. Judged under the Iron Law's intent, not a gate, which is finding 1.
- Neither app service was restarted for the stale `uv`. The deploy that ships the host's certifi fix (below) restarts both.

### Surprises

- **The bulletin's fix doesn't finish the host's exposure.** Both deployed venvs carry certifi 2026.07.22, which still trusts `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, and httpx reads certifi, not the system store. That needs a lock bump and a deploy: CannObserv/status#58. `probe.sh`'s "outside apt" and language-dependency classes are where a bulletin that names a root store would need it read.

## Session 2026-10-23 — co-index (a bulletin's out-of-cycle window)

Host repo: CannObserv/index (public); tracking issue CannObserv/index#12; cohort coordination CannObserv/provisioner#77 (Tailscale TS-2026-013). The host's second run under the scripts, after 2026-10-08's.

### Environment

- `exe-dev-exeuntu`, generation newer, the same host as 2026-10-08's entry.
- The knob is `posture scheduled`, with windows Tue–Thu 05:15–11:45 only. It has `origin pkgs.tailscale.com follow` and `hold tailscale tailscale`, scoped by apt pins (site at 100; `tailscale` and its keyring at 600).

### Readings

- Before: `tailscale version --daemon` 1.104.1 (go1.27.1), client and daemon. `tailscaled` had been active since 2026-10-08.
- `probe.sh --refresh-into`: Tailscale was the only third-party package pending, alongside 42 security packages and 12 `-updates` packages.
- `probe.sh --lane origin:pkgs.tailscale.com --dry-run-into`: `count=1`, 92 s, `origin_left` empty. The lane's `Package-Blacklist` skipped every other pending package.
- The needrestart proof printed `Disabling Ubuntu mode, explicit restart mode configured` and listed nothing.
- **The first bulk was refused at the gate:** `inflight` printed 121, which was a client's index run writing to Qdrant. It drained to 0 in 5 minutes, and the second bulk passed.
- **The bulk** (14:03–14:05Z) placed the `tailscale` hold, and unattended-upgrade had nothing to do (`nothing_to_do: true`, 49 s). Health passed 2/2.
- **The `tailscale` step** (14:13:53–14:16:56Z):
  - It released the hold and upgraded `tailscale` alone in 101 s, against a gate span of 392 s.
  - It stopped `qdrant-cert-renew.timer` and started it again.
  - `tailscaled`: `got signal terminated` at 14:14:46.403Z, `Starting -> Running` at 14:14:48.580Z. **The gap was ~2.2 s**, matching co-provisioner (2.0 s, 2.2 s), co-processor (2.3 s) and co-status (2.2 s).
- After:
  - Client and daemon 1.104.2, go1.27.3, with a new `MainPID` and `ActiveEnterTimestamp`.
  - Qdrant's and Ollama's PIDs were unchanged, with 0 restarts. Health passed 2/2 over the tailnet name.
  - needrestart's list after the step was empty. There was no `reboot-required`.

### What the skill got wrong or lacked

1. **The gate has no out-of-cycle window.** `policy.md` routes a Tailscale bulletin into "an out-of-cycle window: `apply.sh --lane origin:<origin>`", but `apply.sh` applies the `window` check to every lane. The knob's grammar has no window that isn't weekly.
   - The run happened on a Friday, outside every window. The only way in was a knob edit committed for the run, `window Fri 13:55-15:55`, reverted after it (CannObserv/index `e0339be`, `4baebb0`).
   - A weekday line reopens every week until someone removes it. Forgetting the revert would silently widen the host's monthly posture.
   - `--config` with a scratch copy of the knob would also pass the gate, but no record would show the window had been opened.
   - Proposed: a dated window, `window <YYYY-MM-DD> <HH:MM-HH:MM>`, which expires by itself and stays in the knob's history. The `quiet` and `inflight` checks still apply. Alternatively, an `--out-of-cycle <ref>` flag on an origin lane only, which records the reference in the run and still checks `quiet` and `inflight`.
2. **With the origin's only package in a hold group, the bulk takes nothing.** The `origin:` lane's candidates are the origin's packages only, and `hold tailscale tailscale` holds all of them. So the bulk refreshed the lists, recorded the before-versions, held `tailscale` and upgraded nothing. Then the held step did the work. That made two approvals, two gate passes and two reprobes for one package.
   - The bulk's record has value. What's missing is any warning: neither the dry run nor the bulk's plan says it will take nothing.
   - Proposed: when an origin lane's every pending package falls in a hold group, the dry run's summary and the bulk's JSON say so, and name the held step that will take them. Then the owner approves the bulk knowing it is bookkeeping.

### Decisions

- **The origin lane, not a hand run,** because the knob follows the origin. That kept the gate, the before-versions, the reprobe and the run directory (`/var/backups/patching-hosts-20261023T135839Z`).
- **A committed, reverted window line over a scratch `--config`,** so git records that the window was opened.
- **No recovery point.** The knob declares no datastore, and the knob's own note asks for a Qdrant snapshot only before a step that stops Qdrant. Nothing in the set does: both units order `After=` tailscaled only.
- **A Friday afternoon, outside clients' near-silent hours.** This is a `dev` host, and an outage only degrades search. The `inflight` gate covers a client's index run, and it caught one.

### Surprises

- None in the step itself: it matched the four hosts before it.
- The inflight gate refused a real index run on its first try, and released after one drain. That's the first time it held off live work on this host.
````

epic.title: Epic: TypeSafe advisory judgments across the skills (#435–#447)
epic.goal: Turns the thirteen TypeSafe proposals (#435–#447) into opt-in, advisory steps in the skills they name. Each step calls TypeSafe's Jev model for a narrow typed judgment, and none changes a verdict, a gate or a GitHub write. Done when every proposal has either shipped with its agreement measured on a labelled set, or been closed or parked with its measurement as the reason.

scope.text:
- Every TypeSafe step is advisory. It never changes an existing script's verdict or exit code, never passes or fails a gate, and never writes to GitHub. Proposed at creation.
- No network in the pytest suite. Structural tests use a fake transport, and live calls run only under `-m integration` (billed, never gated). Proposed at creation.

- A proposal whose measurement shows no useful agreement is closed as not planned, with the numbers. That is a successful outcome for this epic, not a failure. Proposed at creation.
- **A deterministic script may change behaviour only by an explicit operator decision,** with its effect measured on real files: #441's CommonMark fence fix across `check-counts.sh`, `check-seams.sh` and `prove-no-loss.sh` (decided 2026-10-22; 1 report changed in 725 files, in an archival plan). item.title: coordinating-epics: process-log entry — 2026-10-23 processor (close)
item.body:
A process-log entry for `coordinating-epics`, from a run on a host that consumes this repo as a submodule. The process-log rules send it here as an issue, because writing it in the vendored copy would leave the host with a modified submodule. The host repo, CannObserv/processor, is public, so the entry names it.

This is the **second half** of the run already logged as `process-log/2026/2026-10-12-processor.md`: from the parking lot (2026-10-11) to the operator's close (2026-10-23). Findings F140–F178 are on #348.

**Please add** the entry below as `process-log/2026/2026-10-23-processor.md`, and this row to `process-log/2026/index.md`:

| [2026-10-23](2026-10-23-processor.md) | CannObserv/processor#24 (close) | The parking-lot half: 3 triggered bumps, the skill adopted mid-run on a live body, 7 new issues (a security tier as a sibling's canary), a child correcting the coordinator's own triage. Closed by the operator with one item continuing alone; F140–F178 |

**New candidates for #404** (each also on #348):
- **F169**, with F142: lint refuses a cross-repo comment link the epic's token can't read. Resolve with `GH_TOKEN_<REPO>`, or downgrade to a note.
- **F166:** the usage text should say that placeholders (`{now}`, `{today}`, `{checked}`, `{last_seen}`) expand in every op, not only in `log`. This corrects F161.
- **F172:** an "awaiting" convention for outside readings, separate from blockers.
- **F177:** a disposition (`not planned`, `out of epic`) that the count derivation reads separately from `[x]`.
- **F176:** close-out.md should sweep the epic's Milestones and watch blocks for facts a surviving item depends on, and copy them onto that issue.

---

## Session 2026-10-23 — CannObserv/processor#24 (parking lot to close)

The second half of the run in [2026-10-12-processor.md](2026-10-12-processor.md). The epic had been a parking lot since 2026-10-11, with three items waiting on upstream releases and one on a broker decision. Over the next twelve days, every trigger but one fired. The epic adopted this skill's v1 scripts mid-run. New issues reopened active work three times, including a security tier. The operator closed the epic on 2026-10-23, with one item left to continue alone. Findings F140–F178 are on [#348](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/issues/348), cited `processor#24-F<n>`.

### Shape

- **Way in:** a parking lot with brief-grade parked lines (F135–F138). Check-ins ran only on a trigger, a new issue, or the operator asking.
- **Children in this phase:**
  - three triggered co-core bumps: #29, #21, #37;
  - the skill adoption, #52;
  - seven new issues: #57, #58, #62, #65, #66, #67, #70. Three were filed by the coordinator: #66 from a measurement, #67 under a rule it had set, #70 from a closed child's open list.
- **Check-ins:** about 14, from 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-23.
- **End:** closed by the operator with #54 alone, which waits on a broker window gated by another issue. 26 lines were resolved (25 shipped, plus #70 not planned), and 1 was out of the epic.

### What was different

- **The skill was adopted mid-run, on a live legacy body.** A pre-flight against a copy passed, but the dry-run diff against the live body showed a split header. Reading the diff, not the exit code, caught it (F140, F141, F144).
- **Upstream coordinators did much of the brief.** cannobserv's coordinator replayed Processor's own corpus through each release and posted the moved goldens on the parked issue. So the coordinator verified rather than derived (F154, F155).
- **Pre-approved cross-repo posts.** The operator approved one child's posts in advance. The approval was recorded on the child, with its order, stop conditions and scope (F157).
- **A security tier arrived through a sibling's rollout.** co-processor was the cohort's Tailscale canary. A second exposure the issue mentioned only in passing (a venv's certifi) was measured here, live, and filed (F167, F171).
- **The coordinator's own triage was corrected by a child.** Two flaps it had called "the same signature" were different kinds of event. A cohort Mayfly questionnaire, answered by 8 peer agents with nothing filed in their repos, found the cause: a host memory-balloon reclaim, then per-VM pauses (F175).
- **The session scratchpad vanished mid-run.** Nothing was lost: the state lived on the epic and in memory (F165).

### Findings that changed the protocol (proposed)

**Verifying**
- For a version bump, the live gate is each source's first post-bump output equal to its last pre-bump output, and the close waits for every source to report (F139, F151).
- A docs-only child is verified against the last runtime-touching commit, not `origin/main` (F163). A host-only child swaps CI and `REVISION` for host reads (F170).
- Close any known limit that only needed time (F160). Before ticking, sweep the child's comments for open items and give each a home (F174).
- When a child feeds an outside status table, check that the row is complete, not just that the post exists (F178).

**Handing off**
- Before applying "coordinate if function X changes", check whose copy of X runs (F156). A brief that departs from a written rule also asks for the rule fix (F158).
- Grep every moving case ID across the test tree, not only the assertion that names it (F155).
- When a vendored skill takes a major version, check every skill it invokes against what's linked (F164).
- Check that each cross-repo venue a brief names is still open (F162).
- A coordinator-filed issue carries its probe, and "Done when" is that probe flipping, plus a control (F171).

**Recording**
- A rule the coordinator sets goes into the epic's governing text word for word, not "a rule was set" (F168, F173).
- Carry outside readings on an "Awaiting" line until they land or are waived (F172).
- At close, copy the facts a surviving item depends on from the watch blocks onto that issue (F176).

### Open suggestions for the scripts

- **One token for every repo:** `scan.sh` 404s and lint refusals on repos the epic's token can't read (F142, F169).
- **The usage text:** say that placeholders expand in every op (F166, which corrects F161).
- A disposition the count derivation reads separately (`not planned`, `out of epic`) (F177).
- An "awaiting" convention for outside readings (F172).

item.title: curating-context: the cohort tags class C as tighten: more often than the documented prune:, and a third of class tags name no heading
item.body:
**What:** [`telemetry.md` § Action tags](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/blob/main/skills/curating-context/references/telemetry.md#action-tags) documents `prune:<section>` as the class-C tag ("tightened in place"). The cohort's ledgers mostly write `tighten:` instead, which the doc doesn't list.

**Measured** (2026-10-23, `.skills/context-metrics.jsonl` in the 9 public CannObserv repos that keep one, plus this repo's):

| | `tighten:` | `prune:` | `demote:` | `delete:` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all 10 ledgers | 124 | 84 | 191 | 3 |

`tighten:` leads in 5 of the 10 (address-validator: 20 against 0). No script reads the verb: `record-telemetry.sh` stores `--actions` as free text, and `score-cohort.sh` doesn't parse it. So nothing breaks today, and nothing notices either.

#435 found this while mining the ledgers for class labels ([correction 3](https://github.com/gregoryfoster/skills/issues/435#issuecomment-6372110302)). It found a second drift there too: **36% of class tags (124 of 348) name no `##` or `###` heading** in the base file. They name a paragraph, a claim or a bullet: `prune:redundant-heading`, `demote:Phase 6 anecdotes`.

**Why it matters:** the doc says the tags are "the only mechanism connecting a token delta to its cause". A roll-up by cause keyed on the documented verbs would miss about 60% of class-C tags. A consumer keyed on headings would miss a third of class tags.

**Options (not decided):**
1. **Document what the cohort writes.** List `tighten:` beside `prune:` as the same class, and say `<section>` may name a sub-heading part. `telemetry.md` is at 9,908 / 10,000 tokens, so it must be a net-zero edit there, or follow a split.
2. **Have `record-telemetry.sh` warn** on a verb outside the documented list. That's a behaviour change to a deterministic script, so it needs its own decision.
3. **Leave it.** Record in the doc that the verbs are free text, so no consumer should key on them.

Found during epic #451's #435 check-in; outside that epic, which adds advisory TypeSafe steps only.

item.title: reviewing-code / shipping-work: lint a consumer's shell scripts with a lock-pinned shellcheck
item.body:
## Context

CannObserv/broker#112 added a shellcheck gate: a step in CI's existing job, and an opt-in `.githooks/pre-commit`. Its review of `scripts/deploy.sh` (#106) had listed shellcheck as *skipped verification*, because shellcheck wasn't installed on the node. Every fix in that review was a trap shellcheck is built for: `set -e` doesn't reach into a command substitution, and a failed `sudo` exits with no message. CannObserv/status and CannObserv/processor ship deploy scripts too.

## What broker landed (the shape to copy)

- `shellcheck-py` in a `lint` dependency group in `uv.lock`, alongside ruff. `dev` includes that group. The lock hash-pins the linux x86_64 wheel that carries the binary. That means no root install, which would be a patching-posture decision, and no hook repo fetched at run time, as the `pre-commit` framework does.
- One selector script, which the hook (staged files) and CI (the whole tree) both call through `uv run --frozen --only-group lint`. Because that skips the project, there is no private wheelhouse to sync.
- Scope: tracked `*.sh` and `.githooks/*`. Symlinks into `skills-vendor/` are skipped, and so is `.skills/doctor.sh`, which this repo's refresh hook rewrites.

## Proposal

1. The `-python-*` review skills' Phase 3.5 runs `bash scripts/shellcheck.sh` when the consumer has one. When it doesn't, the review says "shellcheck: not configured" instead of skipping the step silently.
2. Optionally, the selector and hook become a vendored template, installed the way `install-cadence.sh` installs its workflow.

## Measured upstream (2026-10-23, shellcheck 0.11.0 and 0.9.0)

`.skills/doctor.sh` at broker `8c360d7`: 0 findings on both versions. Nothing to fix upstream today; this is about scope only.
